questions.question: A student drew a mechanism for nitrobenzene formation. Describe the three changes needed to correct it. The student's diagram is only in the PDF.
questions.answer: Change 1: the first curly arrow must start from the delocalised ring (pi electrons) and end on the N atom of NO2+, not the other way round. Change 2: the intermediate must be a horseshoe covering five carbons with a + inside, not a full circle, because the carbon bonded to H and NO2 is sp3. Change 3: the last curly arrow must start from the C-H bond (not from the H atom) and go into the ring to restore the delocalised ring and release H+.
steps: Curly arrows show electron pairs moving from the electron-rich ring (nucleophile) to the electron-deficient NO2+ (electrophile), so the student's first arrow is drawn in the wrong direction.
Correct first step: arrow from inside the benzene ring to the N of NO2+, forming a C-N bond.

The intermediate has one sp3 carbon (bearing H and NO2) that breaks the delocalisation: draw a partial ring (horseshoe) over the other five carbons with a + inside, with H and NO2 both on the sp3 carbon.
Final step: curly arrow from the C-H bond into the ring, so the electrons restore the delocalised ring and H+ leaves; the arrow must start at the bond, not at the H atom.

questions.question: Give the reagents for Step 2, the conversion of nitrobenzene into phenylamine.
questions.answer: Tin (Sn) with concentrated hydrochloric acid (heat under reflux), then NaOH added to liberate the amine.
steps: Nitrobenzene is reduced to phenylamine, so the NO2 group becomes NH2.
Sn and concentrated HCl are the standard reducing system.
NaOH is added at the end to neutralise the acid and release free phenylamine.

questions.question: Explain why phenylamine is a weaker base than ammonia.
questions.answer: The N lone pair in phenylamine is delocalised into the benzene ring, so it is less available to accept H+ than the localised lone pair in NH3.
steps: The N lone pair of phenylamine overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring.
This delocalisation spreads the electron density, so the lone pair is held less tightly on N.
Less electron density is available on N to accept a proton.
NH3 has a localised lone pair, so it is the stronger base.

questions.question: State what is seen when a few drops of aqueous phenylamine are added to an aqueous solution containing Cu2+ ions.
questions.answer: A pale blue precipitate forms (copper(II) hydroxide).
steps: Phenylamine is a weak base and produces a small amount of OH- in water.
Cu2+ + 2OH- gives Cu(OH)2.
Cu(OH)2 is an insoluble pale blue precipitate.

questions.question: Give the reagents and conditions for Step 1 in the synthesis of azo violet from 1-amino-4-nitrobenzene.
questions.answer: Sodium nitrite and cold dilute hydrochloric acid at about 0-5 C (diazotisation).
steps: The primary aromatic amine is converted to a diazonium ion.
NaNO2 reacts with HCl to form nitrous acid in situ.
The temperature is kept at 0-5 C so the diazonium ion does not decompose.

questions.question: Deduce the structure of the organic compound that reacts with the diazonium ion in Step 2 to form azo violet.
questions.answer: Benzene-1,3-diol (resorcinol), C6H4(OH)2 with the two OH groups meta to each other.
steps: Step 2 is a coupling reaction: the diazonium ion attacks an activated benzene ring and replaces one ring H, so the coupling partner is azo violet with the N=N-C6H4NO2 group replaced by H.
In azo violet the ring carries two OH groups meta to each other (positions 1 and 3), and the azo group is on C4, ortho to one OH and para to the other.
Removing the azo group leaves C6H4(OH)2, benzene-1,3-diol (coupling is carried out in alkaline solution).

questions.question: Give a reason why azo violet exists as geometric isomers.
questions.answer: The N=N double bond restricts rotation, and each N atom carries two different groups, giving E/Z isomers.
steps: The N=N double bond cannot rotate freely.
Each nitrogen in the N=N bond is bonded to a different group.
So the groups can be arranged on the same side (Z) or opposite sides (E).

questions.question: Complete the diagram to show the other optical isomer of phenylalanine.
questions.answer: Draw the mirror image: H on the vertical plain bond at the top, CH2C6H5 on the dashed bond going up to the left, COOH on the wedge bond going down to the left, and H2N on the plain bond going down to the right.
steps: Optical isomers (enantiomers) are non-superimposable mirror images, so every group is reflected across the mirror line.
Reflection swaps left and right but keeps the bond types: the dashed CH2C6H5 bond goes to the left, the wedge COOH bond goes to the left, and the plain NH2 bond goes to the right.
The H stays at the top on the vertical bond because it lies on the mirror line.

questions.question: A solution contains 19.6 g dm-3 of Cr2(SO4)3 (Mr 392). Options A 0.05, B 0.10, C 0.15, D 0.25 are given. The question wording is missing from the text.

questions.question: An element has configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d5 4s1. What is the maximum oxidation number shown in its compounds? A +1, B +5, C +6, D +7.
questions.answer: C (+6): the element is chromium, which reaches +6 in CrO4 2- and Cr2O7 2-.
steps: Counting electrons gives 24, so the element is chromium (Cr).
Chromium's common compounds include Cr(VI) in chromate and dichromate.
Maximum oxidation state is +6; +7 is not seen for chromium.
Answer C.

questions.question: Write the equation for the reduction of holmium(III) fluoride, HoF3, by calcium (state symbols not required).
questions.answer: 2HoF3 + 3Ca to 2Ho + 3CaF2
steps: Ho is reduced from +3 to 0 and Ca is oxidised from 0 to +2.
Balance F: 6 F on the left, so 3CaF2 is needed.
Balance Ca: 3 Ca on the left.
Balance Ho: 2 Ho on the right.

questions.question: Suggest a reason why gadolinium has configuration [Xe]4f7 5d1 6s2 rather than [Xe]4f8 6s2.
questions.answer: A half-filled 4f7 sub-shell is particularly stable, so one electron moves into 5d.
steps: The 4f7 sub-shell is exactly half-filled.
Half-filled sub-shells have extra stability from exchange energy.
This stability outweighs the cost of promoting one electron to 5d.

questions.question: Complete the electronic configuration of Sm3+.
questions.answer: [Xe] 4f5
steps: Sm (Z = 62) has configuration [Xe]4f6 6s2.
Sm3+ loses 3 electrons: both 6s electrons and one 4f electron.
So Sm3+ is [Xe]4f5.

questions.question: Explain why the ionic radius of Tm3+ (0.095 nm) is less than that of Ce3+ (0.111 nm).
questions.answer: Tm has more protons, so greater nuclear charge pulls the electrons in more strongly; 4f electrons shield poorly, giving the lanthanide contraction.
steps: Across the lanthanides the nuclear charge increases by one proton per element.
Added 4f electrons shield each other poorly.
The effective nuclear charge on the outer electrons increases, so the ion shrinks.
Tm3+ therefore has a smaller radius than Ce3+.

questions.question: Suggest why lanthanide complex ions can contain more ligands than transition metal complex ions.
questions.answer: Lanthanide ions are large and their 4f orbitals do not take part in bonding, so bonding is largely electrostatic and non-directional, allowing higher coordination numbers.
steps: Lanthanide ions have large radii, leaving room for more ligands around them.
The 4f orbitals are buried and do not form strong directional bonds.
So bonding is mainly electrostatic, and more ligands can pack around the ion.

questions.topic: Empirical Formula of Ceric Ammonium Nitrate
questions.question: Hydrated cerium(IV) ammonium nitrate contains 23.97% Ce, 19.18% N, 2.05% H and 54.80% O by mass. Calculate the empirical formula and hence the overall formula showing Ce4+, NH4+, NO3- and water.
questions.answer: Empirical formula CeN8H12O20; overall formula (NH4)2[Ce(NO3)6].2H2O.
steps: Divide each % by its Ar: Ce 0.1711, N 1.369, H 2.034, O 3.425 (mol per 100 g).
Divide by 0.1711: Ce 1, N 8, H 12, O 20, so the empirical formula is CeN8H12O20.
Two NH4+ give N2H8, the six NO3- give N6O18, so the remaining H4O2 is two H2O.
Overall formula: (NH4)2[Ce(NO3)6].2H2O.

questions.question: Organic compound X (C7H16O) is not oxidised by acidified dichromate but gives a red colour with cerium(IV) ammonium nitrate, and exists as optical isomers. Deduce a possible structure of X and justify.
questions.answer: 3-methylhexan-3-ol, CH3CH2CH2C(OH)(CH3)CH2CH3 (a tertiary alcohol with four different groups on C3).
steps: Not oxidised by dichromate, so X is a tertiary alcohol (no H on the C bearing OH).
CAN gives a red colour with tertiary alcohols, consistent with X being an alcohol.
Optical isomers need a chiral carbon with four different groups.
In 3-methylhexan-3-ol, C3 carries OH, CH3, ethyl and propyl, all different, so it is chiral.

questions.question: 0.800 g of crushed tablets is hydrolysed to 4-aminophenol and made up to 100.0 cm3. 25.0 cm3 aliquots are titrated with 0.100 mol dm-3 Ce4+ (mean titre 21.70 cm3). Calculate the percentage by mass of paracetamol.
questions.answer: 82.0% (3 significant figures).
steps: 4-aminophenol is oxidised by 2 Ce4+ per molecule (2 electrons lost), so moles 4-aminophenol in 25.0 cm3 = 1.085 x 10^-3 mol.
In 100.0 cm3 there is 4.340 x 10^-3 mol, equal to paracetamol moles (1:1 hydrolysis).
Mass paracetamol = 4.340 x 10^-3 x 151.2 = 0.656 g.

questions.topic: Species Not Acting as a Ligand
questions.question: Which of the following species will not act as a ligand in the formation of a complex ion? The options are in the PDF and are shown in the figure below.
questions.answer: D: NH4+
steps: A ligand must donate a lone pair to the metal ion to form a dative (coordinate) bond.
CH3NH2, CN- and NH3 each have a lone pair on N (or C in CN-).
NH4+ has no lone pair (all four N-H bonds use the N electrons), so it cannot act as a ligand.

questions.question: Describe a chemical test, with the result, that could distinguish the Dewar structure from benzene.
questions.answer: Add bromine water: the Dewar structure (which has C=C bonds) decolourises it, whereas benzene does not.
steps: Dewar benzene contains two C=C double bonds.
Bromine water is decolourised by C=C bonds (addition reaction).
Benzene has delocalised electrons and does not decolourise bromine water at room temperature.
Result: orange bromine water turns colourless with Dewar benzene only.

questions.question: State one similarity and one difference in the low-resolution proton NMR spectra of the Ladenburg structure and benzene, using Data Booklet data.
questions.answer: Similarity: both show one peak because all six H are equivalent. Difference: Ladenburg H are on saturated carbons, appearing at about 0.5-2 ppm rather than the aromatic 6-9 ppm of benzene.
steps: In the Ladenburg structure all six C-H environments are equivalent, as in benzene, so there is one peak in each case.
Benzene's H are on sp2 carbons in an aromatic ring: 6.0-9.0 ppm in the Data Booklet.
Ladenburg H are on sp3 carbons, so they appear at lower shift, around 0.5-2 ppm.
So the peak appears at a different chemical shift.

questions.question: Explain how X-ray diffraction shows that benzene has a delocalised structure rather than a Kekule structure.
questions.answer: X-ray diffraction shows all six C-C bond lengths are equal (about 0.139 nm), intermediate between C-C and C=C, so there are no alternating single and double bonds.
steps: X-ray diffraction measures the positions of electron density and gives bond lengths.
All C-C bonds in benzene are the same length.
This length lies between a C-C single bond (0.154 nm) and a C=C double bond (0.134 nm).
A Kekule structure would show alternating long and short bonds, which is not observed.

questions.topic: Enthalpy Level Diagram for Benzene Isomers
questions.question: Draw a labelled enthalpy level diagram showing the relative stability of the Ladenburg structure, the Dewar structure and benzene, with values -376 and -297 kJ mol-1 for isomerisation to benzene.
questions.answer: Benzene lowest; Dewar about 297 kJ mol-1 above benzene; Ladenburg about 376 kJ mol-1 above benzene.
steps: Isomerisation to benzene is exothermic, so benzene is at the lowest level.
Dewar isomerises with -297 kJ mol-1, so Dewar lies 297 kJ mol-1 above benzene.
Ladenburg isomerises with -376 kJ mol-1, so it lies 376 kJ mol-1 above benzene.
Label each level with its value; Ladenburg is least stable.

questions.question: Give a possible reason why the isomerisation of Dewar benzene to benzene has a lower activation energy than that of the Ladenburg structure.
questions.answer: Dewar benzene is higher in energy and more strained, so less energy is needed to reach the transition state for rearrangement.
steps: Dewar benzene has strained bonds and is less stable than benzene.
Its starting energy is higher, so the energy barrier to rearrangement is lower.
Ladenburg is more strained still, but the barrier to its conversion is higher in this comparison.

questions.question: Use benzene thermochemistry to explain both enthalpy changes of hydrogenation in the table, relative to hex-3-ene (-118 kJ mol-1). The table values are in the PDF.
questions.answer: E-hexa-1,4-diene (-236 kJ mol-1): its two C=C bonds are isolated, so each hydrogenates like hex-3-ene and the enthalpy is 2 x (-118) = -236. E-hexa-1,3-diene (-214 kJ mol-1): its C=C bonds are conjugated, so the pi electrons are partly delocalised, giving extra stability and a less exothermic hydrogenation (22 kJ mol-1 less than -236).
steps: Hex-3-ene has one C=C and releases -118 kJ mol-1 on hydrogenation, so a molecule with two independent C=C bonds should give 2 x (-118) = -236 kJ mol-1.
1,4-diene: the C=C bonds are separated by a CH2 group, so they do not interact and the measured -236 matches the prediction.
1,3-diene: the C=C bonds are conjugated (C=C-C=C), so the pi electrons are delocalised over four carbons, as in benzene, which lowers the energy of the molecule.

A more stable reactant releases less energy when hydrogenated: -214 is 22 kJ mol-1 less exothermic than -236, which is the stabilisation from delocalisation (smaller than the benzene value because delocalisation is only partial).

questions.question: Draw skeletal formulae of three different arenes with formula CH3COC6H4CH3 formed from methylbenzene and ethanoyl chloride.
questions.answer: 1-(2-methylphenyl)ethanone, 1-(3-methylphenyl)ethanone and 1-(4-methylphenyl)ethanone (ortho, meta and para isomers).
steps: The acyl group can attach to the ring at a position ortho, meta or para to the CH3 group.
Ortho: CH3 and COCH3 on adjacent carbons.
Meta: one carbon between them.
Para: opposite carbons on the ring.

questions.question: Identify compound X from its 13C NMR spectrum, using the number of peaks to justify.
questions.answer: X is 1-(4-methylphenyl)ethanone (4-methylacetophenone), the para isomer, because it has 7 carbon environments and the spectrum shows 7 peaks.
steps: Count the peaks: 197, 143, 134, two very close peaks at about 129, 26 and 21 ppm, a total of 7 peaks.
The para isomer has a plane of symmetry: C=O, COCH3, ring CH3, ring C-COCH3, ring C-CH3, the two equivalent C2/C6 and the two equivalent C3/C5 give 7 environments.
The ortho and meta isomers have no symmetry, so each would show 9 peaks.
Peak assignment: 197 C=O, 143 and 134 substituted ring carbons, about 129 two ring CH carbons, 26 COCH3, 21 ArCH3.

questions.question: Complete the mechanism, with curly arrows, for formation of compound X, including the equation for regeneration of the catalyst.
questions.answer: CH3COCl + AlCl3 to CH3CO+ + AlCl4-; the ring attacks CH3CO+, forming an arenium ion; AlCl4- removes H+, regenerating AlCl3 (AlCl4- + H+ to AlCl3 + HCl).
steps: CH3COCl reacts with AlCl3: the C-Cl bond breaks, giving the acylium ion CH3C=O+ and AlCl4-.
The pi electrons of methylbenzene attack the electrophilic carbon of CH3C=O+ (curly arrow from C=C to C).
An arenium (sigma) ion forms, with positive charge delocalised over the ring.
AlCl4- removes H+ from the ring (curly arrow from C-H to the base), restoring the aromatic ring.
Catalyst regeneration: AlCl4- + H+ gives AlCl3 + HCl.

questions.question: Give the structures of the species responsible for the peaks at m/z 43 and m/z 57 in the mass spectrum of butanone.
questions.answer: m/z 43 = CH3CO+ (ethanoyl cation); m/z 57 = CH3CH2CO+ (propanoyl cation).
steps: Butanone is CH3COCH2CH3 (M = 72).
Alpha-cleavage on one side of C=O gives the acylium ion CH3CO+ (43).
Cleavage on the other side gives CH3CH2CO+ (57).

questions.question: Give the structure of one other species expected to give a peak at a different m/z in the mass spectrum of butanone.
questions.answer: CH3CH2+ (m/z 29), or the molecular ion CH3COCH2CH3+ (m/z 72).
steps: Any fragment with a different mass is acceptable.
CH3CH2+ has m/z 29 from cleavage of the C-C bond next to C=O.
The molecular ion has m/z 72.

questions.question: Devise a reaction scheme (no more than four steps) to prepare propan-1-ol from butanone, giving reagents, essential conditions and intermediates.
questions.answer: (1) I2 and NaOH, warm (iodoform reaction) gives sodium propanoate; (2) dilute HCl gives propanoic acid; (3) LiAlH4 in dry ether, then water, gives propan-1-ol.
steps: Butanone is a methyl ketone, so the iodoform reaction removes the CH3CO group as CHI3 (yellow precipitate).
Step 1: I2 with NaOH(aq), warm, gives sodium propanoate, CH3CH2COO- Na+, plus CHI3.
Step 2: acidify with dilute HCl to give propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH.
Step 3: reduce with LiAlH4 in dry ether, then add water, to give propan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2OH.

questions.question: Devise a reaction scheme (no more than four steps) to prepare 2-methylbut-2-ene from butanone, giving reagents, conditions and intermediates.
questions.answer: (1) CH3MgBr in dry ether, then dilute acid, gives 2-methylbutan-2-ol; (2) hot concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4 (dehydration) gives 2-methylbut-2-ene.
steps: Step 1: CH3MgBr (Grignard) adds to the C=O of butanone in dry ether, forming an alkoxide.
Hydrolysis with dilute acid gives the tertiary alcohol 2-methylbutan-2-ol, (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH3.
Step 2: heat with concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4 (acid-catalysed elimination), losing water.
Major product 2-methylbut-2-ene (Saytzeff product); 2-methylbut-1-ene is a minor product.
Distil off the alkene as it forms to shift the equilibrium.

questions.question: Explain what the alternative diagram of caffeine indicates about its bonding and the effect on its structure.
questions.answer: The circle in the five-membered ring shows delocalised pi electrons, so the ring is aromatic: all the ring bonds are the same intermediate length (no separate single and double bonds) and the ring is planar, which stabilises the molecule.
steps: In the passage the ring has fixed C=C and C=N double bonds; the alternative diagram replaces them with a circle in the imidazole ring.
A circle means the pi electrons are delocalised over the whole five-membered ring, with the N lone pair taking part.
Effect on structure: the ring is planar and the C-N and C-C bonds in the ring are equal in length, between single and double bond lengths.
Delocalisation makes the ring more stable (and the N atoms less basic).

questions.question: Suggest why caffeine is a much weaker base than ethylamine, even though its ring has two amine groups.
questions.answer: The N lone pairs in caffeine are delocalised into the ring and C=O groups, so they are less available to accept H+ than the localised lone pair in ethylamine.
steps: Caffeine's nitrogen atoms are part of an aromatic/amide-type ring system.
Their lone pairs overlap with pi electrons in the ring and with C=O groups.
This delocalisation makes the lone pairs less available for protonation.
Ethylamine has a localised lone pair on a simple alkyl amine, so it is much more basic.

questions.question: A 200 cm3 cup of coffee contains about 85 mg of caffeine. Calculate its concentration in mol dm-3 to an appropriate number of significant figures.
questions.answer: 2.2 x 10^-3 mol dm-3 (caffeine C8H10N4O2, Mr about 194).
steps: Mr of caffeine C8H10N4O2 = 194.2 (the formula is from the structure; not printed in the text).
Volume = 0.200 dm3.
Concentration = 4.38 x 10^-4 / 0.200 = 2.19 x 10^-3, i.e. 2.2 x 10^-3 mol dm-3 to 2 significant figures.

questions.question: Caffeine removal is first order with a half-life of 3 to 7 hours. Calculate, to the nearest hour, the minimum time for 160 mg to fall to 20 mg.
questions.answer: 9 hours.
steps: 160 mg to 20 mg is a factor of 8, so 3 half-lives are needed.
The minimum time uses the shortest half-life, 3 h.
Minimum time = 3 x 3 = 9 hours.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Mechanism for Caffeic Acid
questions.question: Draw the mechanism of the proposed electrophilic substitution of 1,2-dihydroxybenzene to give caffeic acid, including formation of the electrophile.
questions.answer: Electrophile (Friedel-Crafts type, e.g.): ClCH=CHCOOH + AlCl3 -> +CH=CHCOOH + AlCl4-. Pi electrons of 1,2-dihydroxybenzene (attacking C4, para to one OH) go to the electrophile carbon; the arenium ion is a horseshoe over five carbons with + inside and H and CH=CHCOOH on the sp3 carbon; AlCl4- removes H+ (arrow from C-H bond into the ring) to give caffeic acid, with AlCl4- + H+ -> AlCl3 + HCl.
steps: Formation of the electrophile: ClCH=CHCOOH + AlCl3 -> +CH=CHCOOH + AlCl4- (the aluminium chloride accepts Cl- from the halogenated acid).

Curly arrow from the delocalised ring of 1,2-dihydroxybenzene to the positive carbon of the electrophile; substitution occurs para to one OH group (an activating, 2,4-directing group), giving the 3,4-dihydroxyphenyl pattern of caffeic acid.
Intermediate: horseshoe over five ring carbons with + inside, and H and CH=CHCOOH on the same sp3 carbon.
Curly arrow from the C-H bond back into the ring, with H+ taken by AlCl4-; the ring is restored.
Catalyst regeneration: AlCl4- + H+ -> AlCl3 + HCl. The question does not name the electrophile, so any sensible carbocation that carries the CH=CHCOOH group is acceptable.

questions.question: Deduce the structure of quinic acid that combines with caffeic acid to form chlorogenic acid.
questions.answer: Quinic acid is 1,3,4,5-tetrahydroxycyclohexane-1-carboxylic acid: a cyclohexane ring with C1 bearing both COOH and OH, OH groups on C3, C4 and C5, and CH2 groups at C2 and C6 (SMILES OC(=O)C1(O)CC(O)C(O)C(O)C1).
steps: Chlorogenic acid is an ester, so hydrolysing the ester link gives caffeic acid plus the alcohol part.
The alcohol part is the cyclohexane ring: the carbon that carries the ester oxygen becomes C-OH.
So quinic acid has the same ring as in chlorogenic acid with that O-C(=O)R replaced by OH: C1(OH)(COOH), C3(OH), C4(OH), C5(OH), with C2 and C6 as CH2.

questions.question: Identify and label the other proton environments on the acetoin structure, labelling them B, C etc.
questions.answer: A = CH3 next to C=O (already labelled). B = the CH hydrogen on the carbon bearing OH. C = the OH hydrogen. D = the CH3 group attached to the CH(OH) carbon.
steps: Acetoin is CH3-CO-CH(OH)-CH3, which has four proton environments.
Environment A is the CH3 on the C=O side; the other three are the CH (B), the OH (C) and the CH3 on the CH(OH) carbon (D).
Any consistent labelling of the three remaining environments is accepted.

questions.question: Complete the table to show the splitting pattern in the high resolution proton NMR spectrum of acetoin.
questions.answer: A (CH3 next to C=O): singlet. B (CH-OH hydrogen): quartet. C (OH): singlet. D (CH3 on the CH(OH) carbon): doublet.
steps: Splitting follows the n+1 rule using hydrogens on adjacent carbons.
A: the neighbouring carbon is the C=O with no H, so a singlet. D: next to one CH hydrogen, so a doublet.
B: next to the CH3 (3 H), so a quartet (the OH proton is not coupled because of exchange).
C: the OH proton gives a singlet (broad), so only four of the rows in the table are needed.

questions.question: The melting temperature of impure crystals is measured against the data book value. A same as true value, B higher, C lower, D could be higher or lower.
questions.answer: C: lower than the true value.
steps: Impurities disrupt the crystal lattice.
This weakens the intermolecular forces, so less energy is needed to melt.
The melting range is lowered and broadened, so the measured value is lower.

questions.question: Grignard reagents react with: A water giving primary alcohols, B all aldehydes giving secondary alcohols, C ketones giving secondary or tertiary alcohols, D carbon dioxide giving carboxylic acids.
questions.answer: D: carbon dioxide gives carboxylic acids after acid work-up.
steps: Grignard reagents with water give alkanes, not alcohols (A wrong).
Methanal gives primary alcohols, so not all aldehydes give secondary alcohols (B wrong).
Ketones give tertiary alcohols, not secondary (C wrong).
RMgBr + CO2 gives RCOO- MgBr, which gives RCOOH on acidification (D correct).

questions.question: In the high-resolution proton NMR spectrum of propan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH3, there are: A one singlet, one doublet and a heptet; B one singlet, two doublets and a heptet; C two singlets and two triplets; D three singlets and a quartet.
questions.answer: A: one singlet (OH), one doublet (6H of two CH3) and one heptet (CH).
steps: The two CH3 groups are equivalent: one doublet from coupling to the CH proton.
The CH proton couples to six CH3 protons, giving a heptet.
The OH proton does not split and appears as a singlet.
Answer A.

questions.topic: Molecular Formula of Hydrocarbon from Gas Volumes
questions.question: 25 cm3 of gaseous CxHy is burned in excess oxygen. Cooling reduces the volume by 75 cm3, and KOH reduces it by a further 100 cm3. Determine the molecular formula.
questions.answer: C4H8
steps: KOH absorbs CO2: 100 cm3 CO2 from 25 cm3 hydrocarbon, so x = 4.
Cooling condenses water: contraction = 25(1 + y/4) = 75, so 1 + y/4 = 3, y = 8.
Molecular formula C4H8.

questions.topic: Structures of C4H8 Not Decolourising Bromine Water
questions.question: CxHy did not decolourise bromine water. Suggest two possible structures.
questions.answer: Cyclobutane and methylcyclopropane (both cyclic C4H8 with no C=C).
steps: Bromine water is decolourised by C=C double bonds.
No decolourisation means no alkene, so the C4H8 must be cyclic.
Two cyclic C4H8 isomers are cyclobutane and methylcyclopropane.

questions.question: How many peaks will the 13C NMR spectrum of the hydrocarbon shown have? Options: four, five, seven, eight.
questions.answer: B: five
steps: The compound is 1,1-dimethylcyclohexane: the two CH3 groups are on the same carbon.
The two CH3 carbons are equivalent (1 peak); C1 (quaternary) is 1 peak.
C2 and C6 are equivalent (1 peak), C3 and C5 are equivalent (1 peak) and C4 is unique (1 peak): 5 environments in all.

questions.question: What are the bond stretches responsible for peaks P and Q in the IR spectrum of an aliphatic compound?
questions.answer: D: P is C-H of an aldehyde and Q is C=O of an aldehyde
steps: Q is the strong sharp peak at about 1730 cm-1: a C=O stretch (aldehyde 1720-1740; acids are lower and broader).
P lies at 2700-3000 cm-1 and shows sharp peaks, including the pair near 2720 and 2820 cm-1 that are characteristic of the aldehyde C-H.
A carboxylic acid O-H would appear as a very broad trough from 2500 to 3300 cm-1, which is not present, so options A to C are rejected.

questions.question: Burning a hydrocarbon gives 2.64 g CO2 and 0.81 g H2O. Which could be its molecular formula? A C2H3, B C4H3, C C4H6, D C12H9.
questions.answer: C: C4H6.
steps: Moles CO2 = 2.64/44 = 0.060 mol, so C = 0.060 mol.
Moles H2O = 0.81/18 = 0.045 mol, so H = 0.090 mol.
C:H = 0.060:0.090 = 2:3, so the empirical formula is C2H3.
C2H3 has an odd number of H and is a radical, so it cannot be a stable molecule; C4H6 (2 x C2H3) is the stable option. Answer C.

questions.question: How many peaks are in the 13C NMR spectrum of methylcyclohexane? A one, B three, C five, D seven.
questions.answer: C: five.
steps: Carbon environments: CH3 (1), C1 bearing the methyl (1), C2/C6 pair (1), C3/C5 pair (1), C4 (1).
That gives five distinct environments.
Answer C.

questions.question: Iron reacts with hydrochloric acid to give a pale green hydrated salt A (Mr 198.8). Deduce its formula, showing working.
questions.answer: FeCl2.4H2O
steps: Iron with HCl gives Fe2+, so salt A is FeCl2.nH2O.
Remaining mass 198.8 - 126.7 = 72.1, which is 4 x 18.0 (H2O).
Formula FeCl2.4H2O.

questions.question: Give the formula of complex ion B, formed when salt A dissolves in water.
steps: Fe2+ in water is surrounded by six H2O ligands.
The aqua ion is pale green, matching the description.

questions.question: Complex ion C has six cyanide ligands. Draw its structure, showing its three-dimensional shape.
questions.answer: [Fe(CN)6]4-: an octahedral complex with Fe2+ at the centre and six C-bonded CN ligands at the vertices.
steps: Fe2+ with six CN- ligands gives [Fe(CN)6]4- (charge: 2 + 6(-1) = -4).
Six-coordinate complexes are octahedral with bond angles of 90 degrees.
Cyanide binds through carbon, so each ligand is drawn C-bonded to Fe.

questions.question: Salt E has percentage composition K 35.6%, Fe 17.0%, C 21.9%, N 25.5%. Calculate its empirical formula.
questions.answer: K3FeC6N6 (potassium hexacyanoferrate(III), K3[Fe(CN)6]).
steps: Empirical formula K3FeC6N6.

questions.question: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of complex ion C with chlorine to form complex ion D.
questions.answer: 2[Fe(CN)6]4- + Cl2 to 2[Fe(CN)6]3- + 2Cl-
steps: Fe changes from +2 to +3, so each Fe loses one electron.
Cl2 gains two electrons to form 2Cl-.
Balance: 2 complex ions oxidised, 2 electrons taken by Cl2.

questions.topic: Types of Reaction in Iron Scheme
questions.question: Complete the table to identify the type of each reaction in the iron scheme.
questions.answer: Reaction 2: tick under Ligand exchange only. Reaction 3: tick under Redox only. No ticks under Neutralisation.
steps: Reaction 2: [Fe(H2O)6]2+ -> [Fe(CN)6]4-: water ligands are replaced by cyanide with no change in oxidation state (Fe stays +2), so it is ligand exchange.
Reaction 3: [Fe(CN)6]4- + Cl2 -> [Fe(CN)6]3-: Fe goes from +2 to +3 and Cl2 is reduced, so it is redox.
Neither reaction involves an acid reacting with a base, so neutralisation is not ticked.

questions.question: Complete the left-hand side of the equation for the reaction of a free radical with curcumin by adding curly half-arrows.
questions.answer: Add a single-headed (fish-hook) curly arrow from the dot on T to the H atom of the O-H group, and a second single-headed arrow from the middle of the O-H bond to the O atom.
steps: The radical T. pairs its unpaired electron with one electron from the O-H bond, forming T-H.
Arrow 1: half-headed arrow starting at the dot on T and ending at the H atom (or the O-H bond).
Arrow 2: half-headed arrow starting at the O-H bond and ending at the O atom, where the other bonding electron remains, giving the O radical.

questions.question: Complete the mechanism for one step of the nucleophilic addition of selenide anions to curcumin, adding curly arrows.
questions.answer: Arrow 1: from the lone pair on Se- to the carbon of the C=C that is bonded to Y. Arrow 2: from the C=C bond to the C-C bond next to the carbonyl, forming a new C=C. Arrow 3: from the C=O pi bond onto O to give O-.
steps: Se- is the nucleophile and the C=C carbon bonded to Y is electron-deficient because the C=O group withdraws electrons through the conjugated system.
Arrow 1 starts on the lone pair of Se- and ends on that carbon, forming the C-Se bond.
Arrow 2 starts in the middle of the original C=C bond and ends between the next two carbons, which become C=C.
Arrow 3 starts in the middle of the C=O bond and ends on O, giving the O- shown in the product.

questions.question: Complete the table relating to two M-curc complexes, in which curcumin anions act as ligands.
questions.answer: [Au(curc)2]+: shape square planar and charge on Au +3. [Al(curc)(C2H5OH)2(NO3)2]: coordination number 6 and O-M-O bond angle 90 degrees.
steps: Au: coordination number 4 with 90 degree O-Au-O angles means a square planar complex.
Charge on Au: two curc- ligands give -2 and the complex is +1, so Au is +3.
Al complex: curc is bidentate (2), plus 2 ethanol and 2 nitrate ligands (1 each) gives coordination number 6.
An octahedral complex has 90 degree O-Al-O angles between adjacent donor atoms.

questions.topic: Reagents for Step X in Methyl Red Synthesis
questions.question: State the reagents and conditions needed in Step X of the methyl red synthesis.
questions.answer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) (K2Cr2O7 with dilute H2SO4), heated under reflux (an oxidation of the aldehyde to the carboxylic acid).
steps: Step X converts the CHO group of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde to COOH, an oxidation.
Reagent: acidified potassium dichromate(VI) (acidified potassium manganate(VII) is also acceptable).
Condition: heat under reflux so that oxidation goes to completion.

questions.question: Draw the structure of compound A in the methyl red synthesis.
questions.answer: Compound A is 2-aminobenzoic acid: a benzene ring with COOH and NH2 on adjacent (ortho) carbons.
steps: Sn with concentrated HCl reduces the NO2 group to NH2.
The COOH group is unchanged, so A is 2-aminobenzoic acid (formed as its ammonium salt in the acid and freed with NaOH).

questions.question: State the reagents needed in Step Y of the methyl red synthesis.
questions.answer: Sodium nitrite (NaNO2) and dilute hydrochloric acid, kept below 5 C.
steps: Step Y turns the primary aromatic amine (compound A) into a diazonium chloride (diazotisation).
NaNO2 + HCl generates nitrous acid (HNO2) in situ; the mixture is kept at 0-5 C so the diazonium ion does not decompose.

questions.question: Draw the structure of compound B in the methyl red synthesis.
questions.answer: Compound B is N,N-dimethylphenylamine, C6H5N(CH3)2: a benzene ring bonded to N with two CH3 groups.
steps: Phenylamine reacts with excess CH3I: both N-H hydrogens are replaced by CH3, forming the tertiary amine (plus HI).
Methyl red contains the N(CH3)2 group on the ring, which confirms B.
B then couples with the diazonium ion at the position para to N(CH3)2 in Step Z.

questions.question: Steps Y and Z should be kept as close to 5 C as possible. State why the temperature should be neither higher nor lower than 5 C.
questions.answer: Above 5 C the diazonium ion decomposes (losing N2), lowering the yield; below 5 C the reaction is too slow.
steps: The diazonium ion is unstable and decomposes to phenol and nitrogen above about 5 C.
This would reduce the yield of the azo dye.
Below about 5 C the rate of reaction is too slow to be practical.
So 5 C is the best compromise between stability and rate.

questions.question: Complete the equation for the synthesis of indigotin from 2-nitrobenzaldehyde and propanone in aqueous sodium hydroxide.
questions.answer: 2 C7H5NO3 + 2 CH3COCH3 + 2 NaOH to C16H10N2O2 + 2 CH3COONa + 4 H2O. The blanks on the paper are 2 propanone, 2 NaOH, 2 sodium ethanoate and 4 H2O.
steps: The equation on the paper shows 2-nitrobenzaldehyde (coefficient 2), propanone and NaOH on the left, and indigotin, sodium ethanoate and water on the right.
Each indigotin (C16H10N2O2) uses two aldehyde molecules (14 C) plus 2 C from propanone, so two propanone molecules are used and the other 4 C leave as two CH3COONa.
Sodium balance: 2 CH3COONa needs 2 NaOH.
Balance H and O to get 4 H2O.

questions.question: Calculate the mass of 2-nitrobenzaldehyde needed to make 10.0 g of indigotin at 85.0% yield.
steps: Mr indigotin C16H10N2O2 = 262.3; moles = 10.0/262.3 = 0.0381 mol.
Two 2-nitrobenzaldehyde (Mr 151.1) per indigotin: theoretical 0.0763 mol.
Corrected for 85.0% yield: 0.0763/0.850 = 0.0897 mol.

questions.question: Give the structure of the organic product of hydrolysis of coumarin 440 with excess aqueous NaOH.
questions.answer: Ring-opened disodium salt: the benzene ring (NH2 para to the side chain) carries O- Na+ and the side chain C(CH3)=CH-COO- Na+ on adjacent carbons, i.e. Na+ -O-C6H3(NH2)-C(CH3)=CH-COO- Na+.
steps: Coumarin 440 contains a cyclic ester (lactone), so hot aqueous NaOH hydrolyses the ester bond.
The ring opens to give a carboxylate (COO- Na+) and a phenoxide (O- Na+) on the benzene ring.
Excess NaOH is used so both acidic groups end up as sodium salts; the C=C and NH2 are unchanged.

questions.topic: Condensation of Coumarin 440 with Ethanoyl Chloride
questions.question: Give the structure of the organic product of condensation of coumarin 440 with ethanoyl chloride.
questions.answer: The amide: coumarin 440 with NH2 replaced by NHCOCH3 (the 7-ethanoylamino compound, N-substituted ethanamide), plus HCl.
steps: The NH2 group of coumarin 440 acts as a nucleophile towards the C=O carbon of ethanoyl chloride.
Cl- is lost as HCl and an N-C(=O)CH3 amide link forms; the rest of the molecule (lactone, C=C) is unchanged.

questions.question: What is the minimum volume of O2 at r.t.p. needed for complete combustion of 9.2 g of C3H8O3 (Mr 92)? A 4.8, B 8.4, C 12.0, D 16.8 dm3.
steps: Equation: C3H8O3 + 3.5 O2 to 3 CO2 + 4 H2O.

questions.question: Complete combustion of 6.02 g of compound Q gives 18.07 g CO2 and 3.30 g H2O. Determine the empirical formula of Q.
questions.answer: C9H8O

questions.topic: Structure of Compound Q from Tests
questions.question: Deduce a structure for Q from the tests (sooty flame, orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH, silver mirror with Tollens, decolourises bromine water, geometric isomers), explaining each.
questions.answer: Q is cinnamaldehyde, C6H5CH=CHCHO (3-phenylprop-2-enal).
steps: Sooty flame and C9H8O: high carbon content typical of an aromatic compound with a benzene ring.
Orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH: a C=O group (aldehyde or ketone).
Silver mirror with Tollens: an aldehyde, so the C=O is at the end of the chain as CHO.
Decolourises bromine water: a C=C double bond.
Geometric (E/Z) isomers: the C=C has two different groups on each carbon.
Together: C6H5-CH=CH-CHO, cinnamaldehyde.

questions.question: Devise a four-step synthesis converting but-2-ene into ethyl 2-methylbutanoate, giving reagents, conditions and intermediates.
questions.answer: (1) HBr to 2-bromobutane; (2) KCN in ethanol, reflux, to 2-methylbutanenitrile; (3) dilute HCl, reflux, to 2-methylbutanoic acid; (4) ethanol with conc. H2SO4 catalyst, reflux, to ethyl 2-methylbutanoate.
steps: Step 1: but-2-ene + HBr (electrophilic addition) gives 2-bromobutane.
Step 2: KCN in ethanol under reflux (nucleophilic substitution) adds one carbon: CH3CH2CH(CH3)CN.
Step 3: heat under reflux with dilute HCl (hydrolysis of nitrile) gives 2-methylbutanoic acid.
Step 4: heat with ethanol and conc. H2SO4 (esterification) gives ethyl 2-methylbutanoate.

questions.topic: Molecular Formula of Compound Q from Combustion
questions.question: Combustion of 4.91 g of Q gives 14.6 g CO2 and 3.58 g H2O. Show that Q is C10H12O (Mr 148).
questions.answer: C10H12O, shown by moles of C, H and O giving a 10:12:1 ratio, consistent with Mr 148.

questions.question: Deduce the structure of Q from its high resolution proton NMR spectrum, using peak areas, chemical shifts and splitting.
questions.answer: Q is 1-phenylbutan-2-one, C6H5CH2C(=O)CH2CH3 (C10H12O).
steps: Peak areas 5 : 2 : 2 : 3 add up to the 12 H in C10H12O.
7.3 ppm, area 5, singlet: C6H5 (monosubstituted benzene, aromatic H 6.0-9.0 ppm).
3.6 ppm, area 2, singlet: CH2 between the benzene ring and C=O, with no H on neighbouring carbons; it is higher than the usual 2.0-2.9 ppm because it is deshielded by both the ring and the C=O group.
2.4 ppm, area 2, quartet: CH2 next to C=O (2.1-2.6 ppm) with three neighbouring H on CH3 (n+1 = 4).
1.0 ppm, area 3, triplet: CH3 (0.7-1.2 ppm) next to a CH2 (n+1 = 3).
Joining the pieces C6H5-CH2-C(=O)-CH2-CH3 gives C10H12O, so Q is 1-phenylbutan-2-one.

questions.question: A student proposed a mechanism for Step 1. Identify two errors by circling them.
questions.answer: Circle (1) the first curly arrow, drawn from +CH3 to the ring (wrong direction), and (2) the intermediate drawn with a full circle inside the ring (it should be a horseshoe/partial ring covering five carbons with a +).
steps: Error 1: curly arrows go from the nucleophile (the electron-rich ring) to the electrophile (+CH3), but the student drew it from +CH3 into the ring.
Error 2: in the intermediate the carbon bonded to CH3 and H is sp3, so the delocalisation cannot go round the whole ring; a full circle is wrong.

questions.question: State how the errors identified in (a)(i) should be corrected, justifying in terms of the structures.
questions.answer: Error 1: start the arrow inside the ring (the pi electrons) and end it on the carbon of +CH3, because the ring donates an electron pair to the electrophile. Error 2: draw a horseshoe over five carbons with + inside, because the carbon bonded to CH3 and H has four single bonds (sp3) and breaks the delocalised pi system.
steps: The ring has delocalised pi electrons that can be donated, and +CH3 is electron-deficient, so the electron pair must move from the ring to the CH3 carbon.
After the new C-C bond forms, one ring carbon is sp3, so only the other five carbons share four pi electrons.
This partial delocalisation is shown as a horseshoe (open towards the sp3 carbon) carrying the + charge.

questions.question: Give a reason why it is important to keep the temperature below 30 C in Step 2.
questions.answer: To prevent further nitration, which would give dinitro (and trinitro) products instead of the mono-nitro compound.
steps: Methylbenzene is more reactive than benzene, so more than one NO2 group can easily be substituted.
Keeping the temperature below 30 C favours mono-substitution and a better yield of the required product.

questions.question: State the type of reaction in Step 3.
questions.answer: Oxidation (the CH3 group is oxidised to CO2H by alkaline KMnO4).
steps: The side-chain CH3 on the ring becomes CO2H, an increase in oxygen content.
Alkaline KMnO4 is an oxidising agent, so Step 3 is oxidation.

questions.question: Identify, by name or formula, the reagents needed for Step 4.
questions.answer: Tin (Sn) and concentrated hydrochloric acid (heated under reflux), followed by NaOH(aq) to release the free amine.
steps: Step 4 converts the NO2 group to NH2, a reduction.
The standard reagent is Sn with concentrated HCl, heated under reflux (Fe/HCl or H2/Ni are alternatives); NaOH is added after reaction to free the amine.

questions.question: Explain how the structures of ethanoyl chloride and compound A enable them to react to form 2-ethanoylaminobenzoic acid in Step 5.
questions.answer: Ethanoyl chloride has an electrophilic C=O carbon (delta+) and a good leaving group Cl; compound A (with NH2) has a nucleophilic N lone pair that attacks, then Cl- is eliminated.
steps: Compound A is the amine (NH2 group), with a lone pair on N that acts as a nucleophile.
The C of C=O in ethanoyl chloride is delta+ because O and Cl are electronegative.
The N lone pair attacks this carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.
Cl- is eliminated, reforming C=O and giving the amide with HCl.

questions.topic: Volume of Benzene for Overall Yield
questions.question: Calculate the volume of benzene needed to form 5.92 g of 2-ethanoylaminobenzoic acid at an overall yield of 28.2%. Density of benzene 0.879 g cm-3.
steps: Mr of C9H9NO3 = 179.2; moles product = 5.92/179.2 = 0.0330 mol.
Theoretical product = 0.0330/0.282 = 0.117 mol.
One benzene ring per product, so 0.117 mol benzene (Mr 78.1), i.e. 9.15 g.
Volume = 9.15/0.879 = 10.4 cm3 (3 significant figures).

questions.question: Which solvent is used to prepare 2-methylpropylmagnesium bromide? A ethanol, B ether, C pentane, D propanone.
questions.answer: B: ether (dry diethyl ether).
steps: Grignard reagents react with protic solvents such as water and alcohols, so the solvent must be dry and aprotic.
Ethanol and propanone react with the Grignard reagent.
Ether is a dry aprotic solvent that dissolves the reagent.
Answer B.

questions.question: Why are anti-bumping granules added to the flask? A lower boiling temperature, B prevent evaporation, C solvent is flammable, D ensure smooth boiling.
questions.answer: D: to ensure the solvent boils smoothly.
steps: Anti-bumping granules provide nucleation sites for bubbles.
This prevents superheating and sudden violent boiling (bumping).
Answer D.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the circled carbon atom (bonded to Mg) in 2-methylpropylmagnesium bromide? A positive and electrophilic, B positive and nucleophilic, C negative and electrophilic, D negative and nucleophilic.
questions.answer: D: negative and nucleophilic.
steps: Magnesium is less electronegative than carbon, so the C-Mg bond is polarised with C delta-.
A carbanion-like carbon with a lone pair is nucleophilic.
Answer D.

questions.topic: Carbonyl Compound for a Grignard Addition
questions.question: Which compound reacts with 2-methylpropylmagnesium bromide to form 4-ethyl-2-methylheptan-4-ol? A hexan-3-one, B hexan-2-one, C hexan-3-ol, D hexan-2-ol.
questions.answer: A: hexan-3-one.
steps: The product has an isobutyl group (from the Grignard) and an OH on a quaternary carbon.
The carbonyl carbon must carry the ethyl and propyl groups: CH3CH2-C(=O)-CH2CH2CH3.
That ketone is hexan-3-one.
Grignard addition then acid work-up gives the tertiary alcohol, option A.

questions.question: The infrared spectrum of compound X is shown. Which could be compound X? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: benzoic acid
steps: The spectrum has a very broad absorption from about 3300 to 2500 cm-1: the O-H of a carboxylic acid.
There is also a strong C=O peak at about 1690 cm-1.
Benzyl alcohol (B) has no C=O, benzaldehyde (C) and acetophenone (D) have C=O but no broad O-H, so only benzoic acid fits.

questions.topic: Molecular Ion m/z by High Resolution MS
questions.question: The high resolution mass spectrum of a compound is shown. What is the m/z of its molecular ion? Options A 92.0261, B 92.0312, C 93.0339, D 93.0390. The compound structure is in the PDF.
steps: The compound is 2-ethynylfuran, C6H4O (3 ring H and 1 ethynyl H).
The molecular ion (M+) has the same mass as the molecule, so option A.

questions.question: How many peaks will the 13C NMR spectrum of the hydrocarbon shown have? Options: four, five, six, seven.
questions.answer: A: four
steps: The compound is 1,2-dimethylcyclopentane with both methyl groups on wedge bonds (the cis isomer), which has a plane of symmetry.
The two CH3 carbons are equivalent (1 peak) and the two carbons bearing CH3 are equivalent (1 peak).
The two ring CH2 carbons next to them are equivalent (1 peak) and the remaining CH2 is unique (1 peak): 4 peaks.

questions.question: Calculate the percentage composition by mass of the elements in salicin.
steps: Molecular formula from the structure: C13H18O7 (glucose unit C6, ring C6, CH2OH C1; 7 O in total).

questions.question: State the reagents and conditions needed to oxidise salicyl alcohol to salicylic acid.
questions.answer: Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) (K2Cr2O7 with dilute H2SO4), heated under reflux.
steps: Salicyl alcohol is a primary alcohol.
Excess oxidising agent with heat under reflux oxidises it fully to the carboxylic acid.
Acidified K2Cr2O7 (orange to green) is the oxidant.

questions.question: Suggest why the high boiling temperature of salicylaldehyde (197 C) makes it very difficult to obtain by oxidising salicyl alcohol.
questions.answer: The aldehyde is oxidised further to salicylic acid before it can be separated; its high boiling point needs high distillation temperatures, which the alcohol and products also face.
steps: The aldehyde is easily oxidised further to the carboxylic acid under the same conditions.
Distilling it off requires temperatures near 197 C, close to the boiling point of the alcohol.
The alcohol and aldehyde therefore distil together, so separation is poor.
Some aldehyde is lost as the acid, lowering the yield.

questions.question: Write an equation with displayed formulae for the formation of the electrophile from methanoyl chloride.
questions.answer: H-C(=O)-Cl + AlCl3 to [H-C≡O]+ + [AlCl4]-
steps: AlCl3 accepts a chloride ion from HCOCl.
This produces the formyl cation [H-C≡O]+ (the electrophile) and AlCl4-.
Show displayed formulae with the C-Cl bond breaking.

questions.question: Draw the mechanism for the formation of benzaldehyde from benzene using the electrophile from (c)(i).
questions.answer: [HCO]+ attacks benzene to form an arenium ion; AlCl4- removes H+, regenerating the ring, AlCl3 and HCl.
steps: The pi electrons of benzene attack the formyl cation (curly arrow from C=C to C of [HCO]+).
An arenium ion forms with positive charge delocalised over the ring.
AlCl4- removes H+ from the ring, with the C-H electrons returning to restore aromaticity.
Products: benzaldehyde, AlCl3 and HCl.

questions.question: Devise a synthesis of intermediate F from salicylaldehyde and bromoethane as the only organic starting materials, with reagents, intermediates and conditions.
questions.answer: Step 1: CH3CH2Br + Mg in dry ether -> CH3CH2MgBr. Step 2: add salicylaldehyde in dry ether, then dilute acid, to give the secondary alcohol 1-(2-hydroxyphenyl)propan-1-ol. Step 3: dehydrate with concentrated H2SO4 (or concentrated H3PO4) and heat to give F, 2-(prop-1-enyl)phenol.
steps: F has one more carbon-carbon bond than salicylaldehyde plus a C2 unit, so the ethyl group from bromoethane must be added to the CHO carbon with a Grignard reagent.
Step 1: bromoethane with magnesium in dry (anhydrous) ether, reflux, gives ethylmagnesium bromide.
Step 2: the Grignard reagent adds to the C=O of salicylaldehyde; then dilute acid (H+/H2O) gives HOC6H4-CH(OH)CH2CH3 (excess Grignard is needed because the phenol OH also reacts).
Step 3: heating the alcohol with concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4 (or Al2O3) removes H2O to give the conjugated alkene HOC6H4-CH=CH-CH3 (F).

questions.question: Draw a diagram of the complex formed by one salen ligand with a Ni2+ ion, showing the type of bonding involved.
questions.answer: A square planar Ni2+ complex bonded to the two imine N and two phenolate O atoms of the salen ligand by dative (coordinate) bonds.
steps: Salen is a tetradentate ligand with two N and two O donor atoms.
All four donor atoms bond to Ni2+ through dative (coordinate) covalent bonds from lone pairs.
The complex is square planar with the two O atoms and two N atoms in one plane.
Draw two chelate rings, each including Ni.

questions.question: Explain why the salen complex of Ni2+ is much more stable than the aqua complex of the same ion.
questions.answer: The chelate effect: salen is multidentate, so it forms more bonds per ligand and releases more water molecules, increasing entropy.
steps: Salen binds through four donor atoms, forming chelate rings.
Each salen ligand replaces four water molecules, increasing the number of particles in solution.
This gives a large positive entropy change, making the complex more stable (chelate effect).

questions.topic: Percentage Carbon in PET Repeat Unit
questions.question: What is the percentage by mass of carbon in the PET repeat unit? A 57.1, B 62.5, C 65.2, D 66.7 %.
steps: The PET repeat unit is -OCC6H4COOCH2CH2-, formula C10H8O4 (M = 192.2).

questions.question: How many peaks are in the 13C NMR spectrum of benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid? A 2, B 3, C 4, D 6.
steps: Two equivalent C-COOH ring carbons (C1 and C4) give one peak.
The four equivalent ring C-H carbons give one peak.
The two equivalent COOH carbons give one peak; total 3.

questions.question: The repeat unit of another polymer is shown. The polymer is formed from: A single monomer by addition, B single monomer by condensation, C two monomers by addition, D two monomers by condensation.
questions.answer: A: a single type of monomer by an addition reaction
steps: The polymer chain has a backbone made only of carbon atoms, -CH2-C(CH3)(COOCH2CH2OH)-.
This comes from the C=C of one monomer, CH2=C(CH3)COOCH2CH2OH, so the monomer is one type of molecule and the reaction is addition polymerisation.
The ester group is a side chain on the monomer and is not formed during polymerisation.

questions.question: What is the number of peaks in the 13C NMR spectrum of methylbenzene? A seven, B six, C five, D four.
questions.answer: C: five.
steps: Ring carbons: ipso C (1), ortho pair (1), meta pair (1), para C (1) = 4 environments.
CH3 carbon (1).
Total 5, option C.

questions.question: What type of reaction takes place when methylbenzene reacts with concentrated nitric and sulfuric acids? A nucleophilic addition, B nucleophilic substitution, C electrophilic addition, D electrophilic substitution.
questions.answer: D: electrophilic substitution.
steps: The NO2+ ion is the electrophile.
It attacks the aromatic ring, which keeps its delocalised system.
An H atom is replaced by NO2, so it is substitution, not addition.

questions.question: Which expression gives the mass in grams of 2,4,6-trinitromethylbenzene from 10 g of methylbenzene at 85% yield? Mr methylbenzene 92, product 227. A (10 x 85 x 227)/(92 x 100), B (10 x 100 x 227)/(92 x 85), C (10 x 100 x 227)/(92 x 115), D (10 x 115 x 227)/(92 x 100).
steps: Theoretical mass = 10 x 227/92.
Actual mass = theoretical x yield/100 = theoretical x 85/100.
Combined: (10 x 85 x 227)/(92 x 100), option A.

questions.topic: Synthesis of Benzoic Acid from Benzene
questions.question: Devise a reaction scheme to produce benzoic acid from benzene via bromobenzene and then a Grignard reagent, with reagents, conditions and intermediates.
questions.answer: (1) Br2 with FeBr3 catalyst gives bromobenzene; (2) Mg in dry ether gives C6H5MgBr; (3) solid CO2 (dry ice) then dilute acid gives benzoic acid.
steps: Step 1: benzene + Br2 with FeBr3 catalyst (electrophilic substitution) gives bromobenzene.
Step 2: bromobenzene + Mg in dry ether gives phenylmagnesium bromide, C6H5MgBr.
Step 3: add the Grignard to solid CO2 (dry ice), which forms C6H5COOMgBr.
Step 4: add dilute acid (H3O+) to give benzoic acid, C6H5COOH.
The dry conditions are needed to stop the Grignard reacting with water.

questions.question: Draw the mechanism, with curly arrows, for the nitration of benzoic acid to 3-nitrobenzoic acid, including equations for the catalyst's role and regeneration.
questions.answer: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 to NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4-; NO2+ attacks the ring meta to COOH via an arenium ion; HSO4- removes H+, regenerating H2SO4.
steps: Catalyst action: HNO3 + 2H2SO4 gives NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4-.
The pi electrons of benzoic acid attack NO2+ (curly arrow from C=C to N).
The COOH group is electron-withdrawing and directs meta, so attack at C3 gives the most stable arenium ion.
HSO4- (or H2O) removes H+ from the arenium ion (curly arrow from C-H to base).
Regeneration: H3O+ + HSO4- gives H2SO4 + H2O, so the sulfuric acid catalyst is regenerated.

questions.topic: Reagents for Reduction of Nitro Group
questions.question: State the reagents required to convert 3-nitrobenzoic acid into 3-aminobenzoic acid.
questions.answer: Tin (Sn) and concentrated hydrochloric acid (heat under reflux), then NaOH.
steps: The nitro group is reduced to an amine.
Sn with concentrated HCl is the standard reagent, with NaOH added to release the free amine.

questions.question: State a temperature at which the diazotisation of 3-aminobenzoic acid should take place, giving one reason.
questions.answer: About 0-5 C, because the diazonium ion decomposes at higher temperatures (losing N2).
steps: Sodium nitrite and dilute HCl form nitrous acid.
Diazonium ions are unstable and decompose at higher temperatures, releasing N2.
So the reaction is kept at 0-5 C.

questions.topic: Azo Dye from Diazonium and Phenol
questions.question: Draw the structure of the azo dye formed when the diazonium ion from 3-aminobenzoic acid reacts with phenol.
questions.answer: 3-[(4-hydroxyphenyl)diazenyl]benzoic acid: HOOC-C6H4-N=N-C6H4-OH, with the COOH and the N=N group meta to each other on one ring and the OH para to the N=N on the other ring.
steps: The diazonium group sits meta to COOH on the benzoic acid ring.
Phenol couples at the para position to its OH group.
The product has N=N linking the two rings.

questions.topic: Water of Crystallisation in Calcium Benzoate
questions.question: 2.60 g of Ca(C6H5COO)2.xH2O gives 3.89 g of Pb(C6H5COO)2 precipitate. Calculate the molar mass of the hydrated calcium benzoate and hence x.
questions.answer: Molar mass about 300 g mol-1, so x = 1 (Ca(C6H5COO)2.H2O).
steps: Moles of hydrated calcium benzoate = 8.66 x 10^-3 mol (1:1).
Anhydrous Ca(C6H5COO)2 Mr = 40.1 + 242.2 = 282.3.
Difference = 18.0 = 1 x H2O, so x = 1.

questions.question: How would the solubility of cocaine in water and the pH of its aqueous solution compare with benzoylecgonine? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: C: cocaine is less soluble in water and its solution has a higher pH
steps: Benzoylecgonine has a COOH group (cocaine has an ester COOCH3 instead).
The COOH group can hydrogen bond with water and exists as a zwitterion with the amine, so benzoylecgonine is more soluble and its solution is more acidic (lower pH).
Cocaine has only the basic tertiary amine, so its solution is more basic (higher pH) and it is less soluble.

questions.question: How should the solubility of a compound depend on temperature for recrystallisation? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: B: soluble at high temperature and insoluble at low temperature
steps: The compound is dissolved in the minimum volume of hot solvent, so it must be soluble when hot.
On cooling it must crystallise out, so it must be insoluble (poorly soluble) when cold; soluble impurities remain in the solution.

questions.topic: Molar Mass of Coniine from Gas Volume
questions.question: 0.235 g of coniine vaporised at 185 C and 105 000 Pa gives 67.1 cm3 of vapour. Show that the molar mass is 127 g mol-1.
questions.answer: M = 127 g mol-1

questions.topic: Formula of Alkyl Group R in Coniine
questions.question: Deduce the molecular formula of the alkyl group R in coniine, using its structure and molar mass, showing working.
questions.answer: R = C3H7 (propyl); coniine is C8H17N.
steps: Coniine has a piperidine ring with one R group at C2.
The rest of the molecule (ring plus NH) is C5H10N, Mr = 84.
R = 127 - 84 = 43, which is C3H7 (propyl).
Coniine is therefore C8H17N.

questions.topic: Structure of Alkyl Group from NMR
questions.question: Explain why only one of the two possible structures of R can give the low-resolution NMR data in the table.
questions.answer: The data show three proton environments with area ratio 3 : 2 : 2, which fits CH3CH2CH2- (propyl) only; (CH3)2CH- would give two environments with area ratio 6 : 1.
steps: R is C3H7, which can be CH3CH2CH2- or (CH3)2CH-.
The table gives three peaks with areas 3, 2 and 2 (7 H in total), so there are three different proton environments.
Propyl has three environments: CH3 (3 H), middle CH2 (2 H) and CH2 next to the ring (2 H).
Isopropyl has only two environments: two equivalent CH3 groups (6 H) and one CH (1 H), which would give two peaks in the ratio 6 : 1.
The shift of 0.90 ppm (area 3) is typical of R-CH3 and the 1.33 and 1.37 ppm peaks of R-CH2-R, which supports propyl.

questions.question: In the high resolution NMR data for R, proton environment 2 is a sextet. Deduce the splitting patterns for environments 1 and 3.
questions.answer: Environment 1 (CH3): triplet. Environment 3 (CH2 next to the ring): quartet.
steps: R is CH3(1)-CH2(2)-CH2(3)- attached to ring C2, so environment 2 is the middle CH2 with 3 + 2 = 5 neighbouring H, which gives the sextet.
Environment 1 is the CH3, next to the CH2 (environment 2) with 2 H, so n + 1 = 3: a triplet.
Environment 3 is next to the CH2 (environment 2, 2 H) and the ring CH (1 H), so 3 neighbouring H and n + 1 = 4: a quartet.

questions.question: Using a diagram (R for the alkyl group), explain which type of stereoisomerism coniine shows.
questions.answer: Optical isomerism (enantiomers): C2 is a chiral carbon bonded to H, R, the ring CH2 and the ring NH, so the two mirror-image forms are non-superimposable.
steps: The C2 atom of the piperidine ring has four different groups: H, R, CH2 (ring) and NH (ring).
So C2 is a chiral centre.
Two mirror-image forms (enantiomers) are non-superimposable, shown by drawing one as the mirror image of the other with R at the same position.
This is optical isomerism; the two forms rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions.

questions.question: Draw the mechanism for the reaction of benzene with bromine in the presence of FeBr3, including the formation of the electrophile.
questions.answer: Br2 + FeBr3 to Br+ + FeBr4-; the ring attacks Br+ to form an arenium ion; FeBr4- removes H+, regenerating FeBr3 and forming HBr.
steps: FeBr3 polarises Br2: Br2 + FeBr3 to Br+ + FeBr4- (electrophile Br+).
Pi electrons of benzene attack Br+ (curly arrow from C=C to Br).
An arenium ion forms with positive charge delocalised over the ring.
FeBr4- removes H+ from the ring (curly arrow from C-H to FeBr4-).
Products: bromobenzene, HBr and FeBr3 regenerated.

questions.topic: Comparing Benzene, Cyclohexene and Phenol with Bromine
questions.question: Compare and contrast the reactions of benzene, cyclohexene and phenol with bromine, including reasons for the differences.
questions.answer: Cyclohexene adds Br2 rapidly with no catalyst (decolourises bromine water); benzene needs an FeBr3 catalyst and undergoes substitution, keeping its delocalised ring; phenol is brominated rapidly without catalyst at 2,4,6 positions because the OH group activates the ring.
steps: Cyclohexene has a localised C=C; it undergoes electrophilic addition quickly with no catalyst.
Benzene's delocalised pi system is stable, so it needs a catalyst (FeBr3) and undergoes substitution to keep the ring.
Phenol: the lone pair on O is donated into the ring, making it very reactive, so it substitutes at 2,4,6 without a catalyst (white precipitate of tribromophenol).
Reasons: delocalisation makes benzene less reactive; the OH group activates the ring; substitution retains aromaticity.

questions.question: Devise a synthesis of benzamide from bromobenzene, with reagents, conditions and intermediates.
questions.answer: (1) Mg, dry ether: C6H5MgBr; (2) CO2 then dilute acid: C6H5COOH; (3) SOCl2 (or PCl5): C6H5COCl; (4) excess concentrated NH3: C6H5CONH2.
steps: Step 1: bromobenzene + Mg in dry ether gives phenylmagnesium bromide.
Step 2: add solid CO2, then dilute acid, to give benzoic acid.
Step 3: benzoic acid + SOCl2 (reflux) gives benzoyl chloride, C6H5COCl.
Step 4: benzoyl chloride + excess concentrated NH3 (aq or alcoholic) gives benzamide, C6H5CONH2 + NH4Cl.

questions.question: Draw the repeat unit of the polyamide formed from the monomers shown.
questions.answer: -[NH-(CH2)6-NH-CO-C6H4-CO]- (repeat unit, with the CO groups para on the benzene ring; HCl is lost on forming each amide link).
steps: The monomers are a diamine and a diacyl chloride, so condensation polymerisation forms amide (peptide) links and HCl.
Each unit joins N-H of the diamine to the C=O carbon of the acid chloride, losing H and Cl as HCl.
The repeat unit is -NH-(CH2)6-NH-CO-C6H4-CO-, drawn with open bonds at each end.

questions.topic: Melting Points of Polyamides vs Polyalkenes
questions.question: Explain why polyamides have higher melting temperatures than polyalkenes.
questions.answer: Polyamides have hydrogen bonds between N-H and C=O groups on neighbouring chains, which are stronger than the London forces alone in polyalkenes.
steps: Polyamide chains contain N-H and C=O groups.
Hydrogen bonds form between neighbouring chains.
Polyalkenes only have London (instantaneous dipole) forces between chains.
Breaking hydrogen bonds needs more energy, so polyamides melt at higher temperatures.

questions.topic: Carbonyl and Grignard Pair Not Forming Compound Y
questions.question: Which carbonyl compound and Grignard reagent would not react to form compound Y? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: A
steps: Y is a tertiary alcohol: the carbon bearing OH carries cyclopropyl, CH3 and CH2CH=C(CH3)2.
A tertiary alcohol forms from a ketone plus a Grignard reagent; B, C and D are all ketone plus Grignard pairs that give Y.
Option A uses an aldehyde, which would give a secondary alcohol (the carbinol carbon keeps an H, and the Grignard here also has an extra CH3 branch), so A cannot give Y.

questions.topic: Volume Changes in Combustion of But-1-ene
questions.question: When 10 cm3 of but-1-ene is burned in excess oxygen, the volume decreases by x cm3; NaOH then removes CO2 causing a further decrease of y cm3. What are x and y? Options are in the PDF.
steps: C4H8(g) + 6O2(g) -> 4CO2(g) + 4H2O(l): 7 volumes of gas become 4 volumes (water is liquid), a decrease of 3 volumes per 1 volume of C4H8.
CO2 formed = 4 x 10 = 40 cm3, and NaOH absorbs all of it, so y = 40 cm3.

questions.question: What type of reaction occurs with a Grignard reagent? A electrophilic addition, B free radical substitution, C oxidation, D nucleophilic addition.
questions.answer: D: nucleophilic addition.
steps: The carbanion-like C of the Grignard reagent is a nucleophile.
It attacks the electrophilic C of a C=O bond.
This is nucleophilic addition.

questions.question: Benzaldehyde reacts with a Grignard reagent then hydrolysis to form 2-methyl-1-phenylbutan-1-ol. What is the formula of the Grignard reagent? A CH3CH2CH2CH2MgBr, B CH3CH2CH(CH3)MgBr, C (CH3)2CHCH2MgBr, D (CH3)3CMgBr.
questions.answer: B: CH3CH2CH(CH3)MgBr
steps: The product PhCH(OH)-CH(CH3)CH2CH3 has the carbinol C bonded to the phenyl group and to the CH(CH3)CH2CH3 group.
The Grignard supplies the carbon group that becomes the alkyl part, CH(CH3)CH2CH3.
So the Grignard is CH3CH2CH(CH3)MgBr, option B.

questions.topic: IR Absorption Not Expected for Valine
questions.question: Which wavenumber range would you not expect to have an absorption in the IR spectrum of valine? A 3500-3300, B 3095-3010, C 2962-2853, D 1725-1700 cm-1.
questions.answer: B: 3095-3010 cm-1 (sp2 C-H), as valine has no alkene or aromatic C-H.
steps: Valine has N-H/O-H (3500-3300 region) and C-H sp3 bonds (2962-2853).
It has a C=O in the COOH group (1725-1700).
It has no C=C or aromatic C-H, which would absorb at 3095-3010 cm-1.
Answer B.

questions.question: What are the expected splitting patterns in the high resolution proton NMR spectrum of valine for the protons shown in bold?
questions.answer: A: the CH3 protons are a doublet and the (CH3)2CH proton is an octet
steps: Each CH3 couples with the one H on the (CH3)2CH carbon, so n + 1 = 2: a doublet.
The (CH3)2CH proton has 6 H on the two CH3 groups and 1 H on the adjacent CH(NH2) carbon, so 7 neighbours and n + 1 = 8: an octet.
The NH2 and COOH protons exchange rapidly and do not split the other signals.

questions.question: Compound J reacts with NaOH to form an ionic compound, with H2/Ni, and with ethanol/H2SO4. Which could be its structure? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: CH2=CHCOOH
steps: Reacts with NaOH to form an ionic compound: it is acidic (carboxylic acid or phenol).
Reacts with H2 and Ni: it has a C=C double bond.
Reacts with ethanol and H2SO4: it is a carboxylic acid (esterification). Only prop-2-enoic acid has C=C and COOH; phenol, prop-2-en-1-ol and ethanoic acid each lack one of the features.

questions.question: Complete combustion of 5.26 g of A gives 15.3 g CO2 and 4.18 g H2O. A has Mr 136. Show that the formula is C9H12O.
questions.answer: C9H12O

questions.topic: Structures of Compounds A to E
questions.question: A (C9H12O, benzene ring and one side chain) is oxidised to B, which gives a pale yellow solid C with iodine and NaOH. Dehydration gives isomeric alkenes D (with E/Z isomers) and E (without). Draw A to E.
questions.answer: A = 1-phenylpropan-2-ol, C6H5CH2CH(OH)CH3; B = 1-phenylpropan-2-one, C6H5CH2COCH3; C = triiodomethane, CHI3; D = (E)/(Z)-1-phenylprop-1-ene, C6H5CH=CHCH3; E = 3-phenylprop-1-ene, C6H5CH2CH=CH2.
steps: A is a secondary alcohol, so oxidation gives a ketone B (methyl ketone).
B with I2/NaOH gives the iodoform reaction, giving yellow CHI3 (C).
Dehydration of A gives C6H5CH=CHCH3 (D, has E/Z isomers) and C6H5CH2CH=CH2 (E, no E/Z isomers).
Both alkenes decolourise bromine water.

questions.topic: Structure of Isomer F with Six 13C Peaks
questions.question: Compound F is a structural isomer of A with a benzene ring and one side chain, not oxidised by acidified dichromate, with six 13C peaks. Draw F and label the six carbon environments.
questions.answer: F = 2-phenylpropan-2-ol, C6H5C(CH3)2OH (a tertiary alcohol).
steps: Not oxidised, so it is a tertiary alcohol with no H on the C bearing OH.
C6H5C(CH3)2OH: ring has 4 environments (ipso, ortho, meta, para).
Quaternary C-OH (1) and the two equivalent CH3 groups (1).
Total 6 peaks.

questions.question: G is a structural isomer of A with a benzene ring and one side chain, and its mass spectrum has a peak at m/z 107. Deduce the structure of G and justify.
questions.answer: G = 1-phenylpropan-1-ol, C6H5CH(OH)CH2CH3; the m/z 107 peak is C6H5CHOH+ formed by loss of C2H5 (29).
steps: M = 136; 136 - 107 = 29, which is loss of C2H5 (ethyl).
Cleavage of the C-C bond next to the benzylic carbon gives C6H5CH=OH+ at m/z 107.
So the side chain is -CH(OH)CH2CH3 attached to the ring.
G = 1-phenylpropan-1-ol.

questions.question: What is formed when 4-aminophenol reacts with hydrochloric acid? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: HO-C6H4-NH3+ (the amine group is protonated)
steps: HCl is an acid, so it donates H+ to the basic site.
The NH2 lone pair accepts H+ to form -NH3+ (hydrochloride salt).
The phenol OH is far less basic, so it is not protonated, and nothing is deprotonated by an acid.

questions.question: Give the IUPAC name for acrylamide.
questions.answer: Prop-2-enamide
steps: Acrylamide is CH2=CHCONH2, a three-carbon chain with a C=C at C2.
The amide ends the name in -amide; the C=C is -2-en-.
Name: prop-2-enamide.

questions.question: Explain why PAM can absorb large amounts of water, including a diagram.
questions.answer: Amide groups (C=O and N-H) on the polymer form many hydrogen bonds with water; the chains uncoil and swell, trapping large amounts of water.
steps: Each amide group has a C=O (H-bond acceptor) and N-H (H-bond donor).
Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with these groups along the chains.
The polymer swells as water enters and the chains spread apart.
Diagram: show C=O...H-O and N-H...O hydrogen bonds between chain and water.

questions.topic: Open Coil Structure of PAA above pH 8
questions.question: Suggest why PAA exists as an open coil structure above pH 8.
questions.answer: Above pH 8 the COOH groups are deprotonated to COO-, so like charges repel and the chain extends, breaking intramolecular hydrogen bonds.
steps: Above pH 8 the carboxylic acid groups lose H+ to form carboxylate ions COO-.
Negatively charged groups repel each other along the chain.
The chain straightens into an open coil, and the intramolecular hydrogen bonds are broken.

questions.question: Draw the structure of the vinylpyrrolidone monomer used to make PVP.
questions.answer: 1-ethenylpyrrolidin-2-one (N-vinylpyrrolidone), CH2=CH-N(ring) with the ring C=O; formula C6H9NO.
steps: Pyrrolidone is a five-membered ring with N and a C=O next to it.
A vinyl group CH=CH2 is attached to the ring N.
Formula C6H9NO, the monomer of PVP.

questions.question: Calculate the number of monomers needed to make one PVP molecule of molar mass 90 000 g mol-1.
questions.answer: 810 monomers
steps: Mr of C6H9NO = 111.1.
Nearest whole number: 810.

questions.topic: Molecules of PVP in a Tablet
questions.question: A 740 mg tablet contains 4.0% PVP by mass. Calculate the number of PVP molecules in the tablet (PVP M 90 000 g mol-1).
questions.answer: 2.0 x 10^17 molecules
steps: Molecules = 3.29 x 10^-7 x 6.02 x 10^23 = 1.98 x 10^17, i.e. 2.0 x 10^17 to 2 significant figures.

questions.question: State what is meant by the term condensation polymer.
questions.answer: A polymer formed by joining monomers with two reactive groups, eliminating a small molecule such as water or HCl at each linkage.
steps: Monomers each have two (or more) functional groups.
Each link forms a new bond (e.g. amide) by eliminating a small molecule.
Examples: water in polyesters and polyamides, HCl from acyl chlorides.

questions.question: Nylon 6,6 is made from two monomers. Deduce the structural formulae of these two monomers.
questions.answer: Hexanedioic acid, HOOC(CH2)4COOH, and hexane-1,6-diamine, H2N(CH2)6NH2.
steps: The repeat unit -NH(CH2)6NH-CO(CH2)4CO- shows six carbons in each part.
The diamine is H2N(CH2)6NH2.
The diacid is HOOC(CH2)4COOH (six carbons including the two COOH).

questions.question: Caprolactam is converted to nylon 6 by ring-opening polymerisation. Draw two repeat units of nylon 6.
questions.answer: -[NH(CH2)5CO]-[NH(CH2)5CO]-
steps: Caprolactam is a six-membered ring with NH and C=O (C6H11NO).
Ring opening gives -NH-(CH2)5-CO- as the repeat unit.
Two repeat units: -[NH(CH2)5CO]2-, i.e. -NH(CH2)5CO-NH(CH2)5CO-.

questions.question: Give the IUPAC name for salicylic acid.
questions.answer: 2-hydroxybenzoic acid
steps: Salicylic acid is a benzoic acid with an OH group on the carbon next to the COOH.
The COOH carbon is C1 of the ring, the OH is on C2.

questions.question: Name the three functional groups in acetylsalicylic acid.
questions.answer: Ester, carboxylic acid and arene (benzene ring).
steps: The -OCOCH3 group is an ester.
The -COOH group is a carboxylic acid.
The benzene ring is an arene.

questions.question: Write the equation for the reaction of salicylic acid with ethanoic anhydride.
questions.answer: C6H4(OH)COOH + (CH3CO)2O to CH3COOC6H4COOH + CH3COOH
steps: The phenolic OH group attacks one C=O of the anhydride.
An ethanoyl group is transferred to O, forming an ester.
Ethanoic acid is the by-product.

questions.question: 2.00 g of salicylic acid gives a 74.8% yield of acetylsalicylic acid. Calculate the mass formed (Mr 138 and 180).
steps: Moles salicylic acid = 2.00/138 = 0.01449 mol.
Theoretical acetylsalicylic acid = 0.01449 x 180 = 2.609 g.
Actual mass = 2.609 x 0.748 = 1.95 g.

questions.question: Complete the equation for the dissociation of acetylsalicylic acid in aqueous solution.
questions.answer: CH3COOC6H4COOH ⇌ CH3COOC6H4COO- + H+
steps: The COOH group loses H+ in water.
This gives the carboxylate anion and H+.
The reaction is reversible (equilibrium).

questions.question: Explain why acetylsalicylic acid dissociates differently in the acidic stomach than in the slightly alkaline small intestine.
questions.answer: In the acidic stomach high [H+] shifts the equilibrium to the left, so the molecule stays undissociated; in the alkaline intestine low [H+] shifts it to the right, giving more ionised anion.
steps: Stomach: high [H+] pushes CH3COOC6H4COOH ⇌ anion + H+ to the left.
The neutral molecule stays mostly undissociated and can be absorbed.
Intestine: OH- removes H+, so [H+] is low and the equilibrium shifts right.
More of the ionised anion forms, which is more soluble in water.

questions.question: Identify the reagent needed to convert salicylic acid into methyl salicylate.
questions.answer: Methanol (CH3OH) with a concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst.
steps: Methyl salicylate is the methyl ester of salicylic acid.
Esterification uses an alcohol (methanol) with an acid catalyst (conc. H2SO4).

questions.question: Complete the table giving the chemical shift ranges expected for the side-chain protons (OH and CH3) of acetylsalicylic acid and methyl salicylate.
questions.answer: Acetylsalicylic acid: OH (carboxylic acid) 10.0-12.0 ppm; CH3 (CH3COO-) about 2.0-2.6 ppm. Methyl salicylate: OH (phenol) about 4.0-12.0 ppm (broad, often high due to hydrogen bonding); CH3 (COOCH3) about 3.7-4.1 ppm.
steps: Use the proton NMR chemical shift table in the Data Booklet.
The OH in a carboxylic acid (RCOOH) is far downfield, 10.0-12.0 ppm; the OH on a benzene ring (phenol) has a wide range of values.
The CH3 of the ethanoate group (CH3-C(=O)-O) is next to C=O: about 2.0-2.6 ppm.
The CH3 of the methyl ester (-COO-CH3) is next to O: about 3.7-4.1 ppm.
Exact ranges depend on the Data Booklet edition, so check the booklet values.

questions.question: 0.760 g of aspirin tablets is hydrolysed with 25.0 cm3 of 1.00 mol dm-3 NaOH; 25.0 cm3 of 250.0 cm3 solution is back-titrated with 0.100 mol dm-3 HCl (mean titre 16.95 cm3). Determine which brand was analysed from the table.
questions.answer: Brand B (95.4%): the tablets are 95.3% acetylsalicylic acid.
steps: Moles NaOH added = 1.00 x 25.0/1000 = 0.0250 mol.
Moles HCl in titre = 0.100 x 16.95/1000 = 1.695 x 10^-3 mol, so unreacted NaOH in the 25.0 cm3 aliquot = 1.695 x 10^-3 mol, which is 1.695 x 10^-2 mol in all 250 cm3.
NaOH used up in hydrolysis = 0.0250 - 0.01695 = 8.05 x 10^-3 mol.
The equation uses 2 NaOH per aspirin, so moles aspirin = 4.025 x 10^-3 mol.
95.3% is closest to the 95.4% of brand B.

questions.question: A 10 cm3 mixture of methane and argon is ignited. Methane needs 4 cm3 O2 for complete combustion. What is the volume of argon? A 2, B 4, C 6, D 8 cm3.
questions.answer: D: 8 cm3.
steps: CH4 + 2O2 to CO2 + 2H2O, so 1 cm3 CH4 needs 2 cm3 O2.
4 cm3 O2 needs 2 cm3 CH4.
Argon = 10 - 2 = 8 cm3.

questions.question: What benefit does steam distillation give over other distillation methods? A pure distillate, B high distillation temperatures needed, C works for water-miscible molecules, D avoids decomposition of the organic molecule when heated.
questions.answer: D: it avoids decomposition of the organic molecule.
steps: Steam distillation lets the compound distil below its boiling point, because the mixture boils at a temperature below 100 C.
So heat-sensitive organic compounds are not decomposed.
Answer D.

questions.question: Devise a reaction scheme to form butan-2-ol from iodoethane as the only organic starting compound, giving reagents, conditions and equations.
questions.answer: (1) C2H5I + NaOH(aq), reflux, to C2H5OH; (2) K2Cr2O7/H+, distil, to CH3CHO; (3) C2H5I + Mg in dry ether to C2H5MgI; (4) C2H5MgI + CH3CHO, then H2O/H+, to CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3.
steps: Step 1: C2H5I + NaOH(aq) heated under reflux gives ethanol (nucleophilic substitution).
Step 2: oxidise ethanol with acidified K2Cr2O7 and distil off ethanal as it forms (CH3CH2OH + [O] to CH3CHO + H2O).
Step 3: C2H5I + Mg in dry ether gives ethylmagnesium iodide, C2H5MgI.
Step 4: add CH3CHO to C2H5MgI in dry ether, then dilute acid, giving CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 (butan-2-ol) as a secondary alcohol.
Equations are given in each step; dry conditions are needed for the Grignard step.

questions.question: A 1.850 g sample of compound A (thought to be butan-2-ol) is burned. Calculate the mass increase of solid X (water absorber) and solid Y (CO2 absorber) if A is butan-2-ol.
questions.answer: X increases by 2.25 g (water); Y increases by 4.39 g (CO2).
steps: X (water) gains 2.25 g; Y (CO2) gains 4.39 g.

questions.question: Predict a substance that would give the same mass increases in X and Y as butan-2-ol, and give a reason.
questions.answer: Any isomer of butan-2-ol, e.g. butan-1-ol or ethoxyethane (C4H10O).
steps: An isomer has the same formula C4H10O and molar mass.
It gives the same moles of CO2 and H2O on complete combustion.
So the masses absorbed by X and Y are identical.

questions.question: What is the number of peaks in the 13C NMR spectrum of 1,4-dimethylbenzene? A 3, B 4, C 7, D 8.
steps: Two equivalent ring C bearing CH3 (C1, C4): 1 peak.
Four equivalent ring CH carbons: 1 peak.
