Two equivalent CH3 carbons: 1 peak.
Total 3.

questions.question: Name the functional group present in compound X, a liquid that turns damp red litmus blue.
questions.answer: Amine (basic nitrogen group).
steps: Turning damp red litmus blue indicates an alkaline compound.
Organic compounds that are alkaline contain an amine (-NH2) group.

questions.question: 0.493 g of X vaporised displaced 157 cm3 of dry air at 15 C and 103 000 Pa. Calculate the molar mass of X using the ideal gas equation.
questions.answer: 73 g mol-1

questions.topic: Steamy Fumes from Acyl Chloride Reaction
questions.question: Identify the steamy fumes produced when X reacts vigorously with ethanoyl chloride.
questions.answer: Hydrogen chloride (HCl) gas.
steps: Ethanoyl chloride reacts with X, releasing HCl.
HCl fumes in moist air, forming steamy fumes of hydrochloric acid.

questions.question: Suggest the functional group present in the white solid Y.
questions.answer: Amide (C(=O)NH group).
steps: Amines react with acyl chlorides to form amides.
So Y contains the -CONH- group.

questions.question: Y has composition 62.6% C, 11.3% H, 12.2% N, 13.9% O by mass. Determine its empirical formula, showing working.
questions.answer: C6H13NO
steps: Empirical formula C6H13NO.

questions.question: Deduce the structure of Y using the simplified high resolution proton NMR spectrum (peak areas shown in PDF) and the other information.
questions.answer: Y is N-(1,1-dimethylethyl)ethanamide (N-tert-butylacetamide), CH3C(=O)NHC(CH3)3, C6H13NO.
steps: From (b), Y is an amide (C=O and N-H) with empirical formula C6H13NO (Mr 115); the peak areas 9 : 3 : 1 total 13 H, so this is also the molecular formula.
The peak at about 1.5 ppm (area 9) is a singlet: three equivalent CH3 groups on a carbon with no H, i.e. C(CH3)3.
The peak at about 2.0 ppm (area 3) is a singlet: CH3 next to C=O (2.0-2.6 ppm) with no neighbouring H.
The peak at about 7 ppm (area 1) is a singlet: the amide N-H.
Combining the pieces: CH3-C(=O)-NH-C(CH3)3.

questions.question: Draw the structure of compound X.
questions.answer: X is 2-methylpropan-2-amine, (CH3)3C-NH2 (tert-butylamine), Mr 73.
steps: Y forms from X and ethanoyl chloride: CH3COCl + (CH3)3CNH2 -> CH3CONHC(CH3)3 + HCl.
So X is the amine part of Y, (CH3)3C-NH2, which has Mr 73, matching part (a)(ii).
Displayed formula: a central C bonded to three CH3 groups and one NH2 group.

questions.question: Which of the four isomeric esters P, Q, R and S have five peaks in their 13C NMR spectrum? Structures are in the PDF.
questions.answer: C: R and S only
steps: P (ethyl butanoate) has six different carbons, Q (methyl 2-methylbutanoate) has six different carbons.
R (methyl 3-methylbutanoate): the two CH3 on the CH are equivalent, so C=O, OCH3, CH2, CH and (CH3)2 give 5 peaks.
S (propan-2-yl propanoate): the two CH3 on the OCH are equivalent, so CH3, CH2, C=O, OCH and (CH3)2 give 5 peaks.

questions.topic: Esters with No Doublet in Proton NMR
questions.question: Which of the esters will not have a doublet in its high resolution proton NMR spectrum? Structures are in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: P
steps: A doublet comes from a group whose protons have just one neighbouring H.
Q has CH3 on the CH (doublet), R has (CH3)2CH (doublet) and S has (CH3)2CH on the ester O (doublet).
P is CH3CH2CH2COOCH2CH3, with only triplets, a sextet and a quartet, so it has no doublet.

questions.question: Which of the esters could rotate the plane of plane-polarised monochromatic light? Structures are in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: Q only
steps: Only a chiral molecule rotates the plane of plane-polarised light.
Q has a carbon bonded to four different groups: H, CH3, CH2CH3 and COOCH3.
P, R and S have no carbon with four different groups, so they are achiral.

questions.question: Suggest the reagents required for Reaction A, the sulfonation of phenol.
questions.answer: Concentrated (or fuming) sulfuric acid.
steps: Sulfonation of benzene uses concentrated H2SO4 (or SO3 in H2SO4).
Phenol is sulfonated similarly, giving 4-phenolsulfonic acid.

questions.question: Deduce the structure of intermediate compound B, formed by chlorinating 4-phenolsulfonic acid.
questions.answer: 2,6-dichloro-4-sulfophenol (3,5-dichloro-4-hydroxybenzenesulfonic acid).
steps: Cl atoms enter at the two positions ortho to the activating OH group.
The SO3H group remains at position 4 (para to OH).
Hydrolysis then removes SO3H to give 2,6-dichlorophenol.

questions.question: Explain why the reaction of chlorine with phenol occurs under milder conditions than with benzene.
questions.answer: The OH group donates a lone pair from O into the ring, making it more electron-rich and more reactive to electrophilic Cl+, so no catalyst is needed.
steps: The O lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring.
This increases electron density on the ring, activating it.
The ring is more readily attacked by the electrophile (Cl2 is polarised more easily).
So chlorination of phenol needs no catalyst, unlike benzene.

questions.question: Other than the phenol group, name the functional group present in compound C, which loses CO2 on decarboxylation.
questions.answer: Ester (the ethyl ester group, -COOCH2CH3).
steps: On the paper, compound C is ethyl 4-hydroxybenzoate: a benzene ring with an OH group and a -COOCH2CH3 group.
Hydrolysis of the ester gives the carboxylic acid, which then loses CO2 on decarboxylation to give 2,6-dichlorophenol.
So the functional group other than phenol is an ester.

questions.question: Identify three factors organic chemists take into account when considering alternative methods for a synthesis.
questions.answer: Atom economy (or yield), number of steps, and cost/hazards of reagents (safety and environmental impact).
steps: Yield and atom economy: how much of the reactant ends up in the product.
Number of steps and time: fewer steps are more efficient.
Cost, availability and hazards of reagents and waste, including environmental impact.

questions.question: Explain the relative intensities of the peaks at m/z 162, 164 and 166 in the mass spectrum of 2,6-dichlorophenol.
questions.answer: Two Cl atoms with isotopes 35Cl (about 75%) and 37Cl (about 25%) give M, M+2 and M+4 peaks in roughly 9:6:1 ratio.
steps: Chlorine has isotopes 35Cl (75%) and 37Cl (25%).
With two Cl atoms, combinations are 35Cl35Cl (m/z 162), 35Cl37Cl (164) and 37Cl37Cl (166).
Probabilities give approximately 9 : 6 : 1 relative intensity.

questions.question: Suggest why there is a corresponding set of peaks at m/z 163, 165 and 167.
questions.answer: These are M+1 peaks from molecules containing one 13C isotope (about 1.1% natural abundance).
steps: Carbon has a 13C isotope of about 1.1% natural abundance.
A molecule with one 13C atom is one mass unit heavier.
So peaks appear at M+1 positions.

questions.question: Explain how a fuel cell works using the acidic hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell, discussing advantages and disadvantages, with electrode half-equations and another suitable fuel.
questions.answer: Anode: H2 to 2H+ + 2e-; cathode: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- to 2H2O; overall 2H2 + O2 to 2H2O. Advantages: high efficiency, only water produced; disadvantages: cost, hydrogen storage and flammability. Another fuel: methanol.
steps: Hydrogen is oxidised at the anode: H2 to 2H+ + 2e-; electrons travel through the external circuit to give current.
Oxygen is reduced at the cathode: O2 + 4H+ + 4e- to 2H2O.
Protons migrate through the acidic electrolyte (membrane), completing the circuit.
Advantages: continuous supply, high efficiency, only water produced, quiet.
Disadvantages: expensive catalysts (Pt), hydrogen storage and transport are difficult, and H2 is flammable.
Another suitable fuel: methanol (CH3OH) or other small alcohols.

questions.question: Which metal is involved in the formation of a Grignard reagent? A chromium, B copper, C magnesium, D manganese.
questions.answer: C: magnesium.
steps: Grignard reagents are RMgX, formed by reacting an alkyl halide with magnesium metal in dry ether.

questions.question: What best describes the role of a Grignard reagent in increasing the length of a carbon chain? A reducing agent, B oxidising agent, C nucleophile, D electrophile.
questions.answer: C: nucleophile.
steps: The carbon bonded to Mg is delta-, so it attacks electron-deficient carbons.
Grignard reagents act as nucleophiles toward C=O and CO2.

questions.question: Identify the hazard symbol(s) that should be displayed on a box of liquitabs, using ticks. The symbols are shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: Tick the exclamation mark symbol (second symbol, irritant/harmful) only.
steps: The passage says the concentrated detergent can irritate the eyes and skin and cause breathing difficulties if swallowed.
That is the exclamation mark (irritant/harmful) symbol; nothing in the passage suggests the oxidising, explosive or flammable symbols.

questions.question: Draw the structure of poly(ethenol) showing three repeat units.
questions.answer: -[CH2-CH(OH)]3- written as H-[CH2-CH(OH)-CH2-CH(OH)-CH2-CH(OH)]-H with the chain ends shown.
steps: Each repeat unit is -CH2-CH(OH)-.
Join three units head to tail along the carbon chain.
Show the OH on each second carbon.

questions.topic: Percentage of Hydroxyl Groups by Mass
questions.question: Use your structure to calculate the percentage of hydroxyl groups by mass in poly(ethenol).
steps: Repeat unit C2H4O has Mr = 44.05.
One OH group = 17.01.

questions.question: Explain why poly(ethenol) is soluble in water using your answers to (b)(i) and (b)(ii).
questions.answer: About 39% of its mass is OH groups, which form many hydrogen bonds with water molecules, so the polymer dissolves.
steps: Each repeat unit has an -OH group, so the chain is polar.
OH groups are about 38.6% of the mass, a high proportion.
These OH groups hydrogen bond with water, so the polymer dissolves.

questions.question: Give the IUPAC name for glycerol.
questions.answer: Propane-1,2,3-triol
steps: Glycerol is CH2OH-CHOH-CH2OH, a three-carbon chain with three OH groups.
Name: propane-1,2,3-triol.

questions.question: Suggest one way the properties of poly(ethenol) are improved by glycerol, apart from solubility.
questions.answer: Glycerol acts as a plasticiser: it makes the polymer more flexible and less brittle.
steps: Glycerol molecules fit between poly(ethenol) chains.
They reduce the strong hydrogen bonding between chains.
The polymer becomes more flexible and less brittle.

questions.topic: Moles of Glycerol per Tonne of Poly(ethenol)
questions.question: Glycerol is added at 0.110% by volume to 1 tonne of poly(ethenol). Density of glycerol 1.26 g cm-3 and poly(ethenol) 1.19 g cm-3. Calculate the moles of glycerol added.
questions.answer: About 12.6 mol (taking 0.110% of the poly(ethenol) volume).
steps: Volume of poly(ethenol) = 1 000 000 g / 1.19 g cm-3 = 8.40 x 10^5 cm3.
Volume of glycerol = 0.110% x 8.40 x 10^5 = 924 cm3.
Mass of glycerol = 924 x 1.26 = 1164 g.

questions.topic: Structure of Monomer X from Combustion
questions.question: Monomer X (intermediate for poly(ethenol)) gives 95.6 dm3 CO2 (r.t.p.) and 54.1 g H2O per mole burned. Use the IR spectrum (in PDF) to deduce the displayed structure of X.
questions.answer: X is ethenyl ethanoate (vinyl ethanoate), C4H6O2: H2C=CH-O-C(=O)-CH3.
steps: Moles CO2 = 95.6/24.0 = 3.98, about 4 mol, so X has 4 C. Moles H2O = 54.1/18.0 = 3.0 mol, which is 6 H per molecule.
IR peak P at about 1740 cm-1 is C=O in an ester (Data Booklet 1700-1750 cm-1); peak Q at about 1650 cm-1 is C=C (1620-1680 cm-1).
There is no broad O-H absorption at 2500-3550 cm-1, so X is not an acid or alcohol; the strong C-O peak near 1200 cm-1 supports an ester.
The ester O atoms give C4H6O2 (two double bonds), with an ethanoate group on an alkene: CH2=CH-O-CO-CH3.
It polymerises to poly(ethenyl ethanoate), which is hydrolysed to poly(ethenol).

questions.question: State two advantages of using soluble poly(ethenol) laundry bags rather than reusable polyester or nylon bags.
questions.answer: The bags dissolve in the wash, so staff do not handle contaminated linen; and they avoid the need to collect, wash and reuse bags, reducing waste and handling.
steps: Soluble bags dissolve in the wash, so no handling of contaminated bags is needed.
This reduces the risk of infection and skin contact for staff.
No need to collect, wash and re-use bags, so less labour and waste.

questions.topic: Second Reagent and Electrophile in Nitration
questions.question: Identify the second reagent (reacting with concentrated nitric acid) and the electrophile formed in nitrobenzene synthesis.
questions.answer: Second reagent: concentrated sulfuric acid. Electrophile: nitronium ion, NO2+.
steps: Concentrated H2SO4 protonates HNO3, which loses water.
HNO3 + 2H2SO4 gives NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4-.
So the electrophile is NO2+.

questions.question: Draw the mechanism for the reaction of the electrophile with benzene to form nitrobenzene.
questions.answer: NO2+ is attacked by the benzene pi electrons to form an arenium ion; H+ is removed by HSO4- to regenerate the ring.
steps: Curly arrow from a C=C pi bond of benzene to N of NO2+.
An arenium ion forms with positive charge delocalised over the ring.
A base (HSO4- or H2O) removes H+ from the carbon bearing NO2 (curly arrow from C-H to base).
The C-H electrons restore the aromatic ring, giving nitrobenzene.

questions.question: Identify the reagents required to convert nitrobenzene into phenylamine.
questions.answer: Tin (Sn) and concentrated hydrochloric acid, then NaOH.
steps: The nitro group is reduced to NH2 by Sn/conc. HCl.
NaOH is added at the end to liberate the free amine.

questions.question: State the type of reaction occurring when nitrobenzene is converted into phenylamine.
questions.answer: Reduction.
steps: The nitro group gains electrons/hydrogen and is converted into an amine.
So it is a reduction.

questions.question: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of using ethanoic anhydride rather than ethanoyl chloride to acetylate phenylamine, considering hazards and atom economy.
questions.answer: Anhydride is less reactive and safer (no HCl fumes) but has lower atom economy (ethanoic acid is a waste product, about 69% vs about 79% for ethanoyl chloride); ethanoyl chloride reacts vigorously and releases corrosive HCl.
steps: Ethanoyl chloride reacts vigorously with water and amines, releasing corrosive HCl fumes, a hazard.
Ethanoic anhydride is less reactive, so the reaction is easier to control and gives less fuming.
Atom economy: C8H9NO product (135.2) from C6H7N + C4H6O3 (195.2 total) gives about 69%.
From C6H7N + C2H3ClO (171.6 total) the atom economy is about 79%, so the anhydride route is less atom-economical.
Ethanoic acid by-product is less hazardous than HCl but is still a waste product.

questions.question: The overall yield from benzene to N-phenylethanamide is 35.2%. Calculate the minimum volume of benzene needed to make 10.0 g of N-phenylethanamide (density of benzene 0.879 g cm-3).
steps: Mr of C8H9NO = 135.2; moles product = 10.0/135.2 = 0.0740 mol.
Theoretical benzene = 0.0740/0.352 = 0.210 mol (one benzene per product).
Mass benzene = 0.210 x 78.1 = 16.4 g.

questions.question: Explain why the nitration of phenol needs much milder conditions than nitrobenzene formation.
questions.answer: The OH group donates electron density into the ring, activating it so the weaker dilute nitric acid can nitrate it at low temperature.
steps: The O lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring.
This increases the ring's electron density and reactivity.
So dilute HNO3 at room temperature is enough.

questions.question: Draw the mechanism for the formation of methylbenzene from benzene and chloromethane. The equations for the formation of the electrophile and for the regeneration of the catalyst are given in the figure.
questions.answer: CH3Cl + AlCl3 to CH3+ + AlCl4-; the ring attacks CH3+ to form an arenium ion; AlCl4- removes H+ to give methylbenzene, regenerating AlCl3 (AlCl4- + H+ to AlCl3 + HCl).
steps: CH3Cl + AlCl3 gives the electrophile CH3+ and AlCl4-.
The pi electrons of benzene attack CH3+ (curly arrow from C=C to C).
An arenium ion forms.
AlCl4- removes H+ from the ring, regenerating the aromatic ring and AlCl3 (with HCl).

questions.question: Explain, with reference to the mechanism, why this step will not produce a single isomer. The step is shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: The product is a mixture of two enantiomers (a racemic mixture), because CN- can attack the planar C=N carbon from either side with equal probability.
steps: The step is nucleophilic addition of CN- to the C=N bond of the imine.
The C=N carbon and its attached groups are planar, so the CN- nucleophile can attack from above or below the plane with equal probability.
The product carbon has four different groups (H, CN, NH2, C6H5), so it is chiral, and the two attacks give opposite enantiomers in equal amounts: a racemic mixture.

questions.topic: Type, Reagents and Conditions of Final Step
questions.question: State the type of reaction, and the reagents and conditions, for the final step of the phenylglycine synthesis. The step is shown in the PDF.
questions.answer: Type: hydrolysis (of the nitrile). Reagent: dilute hydrochloric acid (or dilute sulfuric acid). Conditions: heat under reflux.
steps: The C-N triple bond of the nitrile becomes a COOH group, so the nitrile is hydrolysed.
Reagent: dilute strong acid such as dilute HCl, which converts C-N to COOH and the nitrogen to NH4+.
Condition: heat under reflux.

questions.topic: Structure of Amide from Propanoyl Chloride
questions.question: What is the structure of the amide formed from propanoyl chloride and N-methylpropylamine? Structures are in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: N-methyl-N-propylpropanamide, CH3CH2C(=O)N(CH3)CH2CH2CH3
steps: The secondary amine CH3NHCH2CH2CH3 loses its N-H hydrogen and the acyl group CH3CH2CO- replaces it, with HCl formed.
The amide therefore has N bonded to CH3, CH2CH2CH3 and the propanoyl group C(=O)CH2CH3, and no N-H.
Options A and B still have N-H, and C has the wrong acyl and amine groups; D is correct.

questions.topic: Volume of HCl from Amide Mass
questions.question: If 64.3 g of the amide is produced, what volume of HCl forms at r.t.p. (1:1 stoichiometry)? A 12.0, B 12.2, C 23.9, D 120 dm3.
steps: Amide C7H15NO has Mr = 129.2.
Moles = 64.3/129.2 = 0.498 mol, so 0.498 mol HCl.
Volume = 0.498 x 24.0 = 11.9 dm3, i.e. 12.0 dm3 (option A).

questions.question: Give the empirical formula of raspberry ketone.
questions.answer: C5H6O
steps: Raspberry ketone is HOC6H4CH2CH2C(=O)CH3, with molecular formula C10H12O2.
Divide by 2: empirical formula C5H6O.

questions.question: Draw the mechanism of the Friedel-Crafts reaction of phenol to make raspberry ketone, including electrophile formation and catalyst regeneration.
questions.answer: Electrophile: ClCH2CH2C(=O)CH3 + AlCl3 -> +CH2CH2C(=O)CH3 + AlCl4-. Curly arrow from the ring (para to OH) to the C+; intermediate horseshoe over five carbons with + inside and H and the side chain on the sp3 carbon; curly arrow from the C-H bond into the ring with H+ taken by AlCl4-; regeneration: AlCl4- + H+ -> AlCl3 + HCl.
steps: Electrophile formation: AlCl3 accepts Cl- from the chloroalkane to give the carbocation +CH2CH2COCH3 and AlCl4-.
Curly arrow from the pi electrons of phenol (attack para to the activating OH group) to the positive carbon.
Intermediate: horseshoe over five carbons with +, and H and CH2CH2COCH3 on the same sp3 carbon (para to OH).
Curly arrow from the C-H bond back into the ring restores the ring and releases H+; H+ combines with AlCl4-.
Catalyst regeneration: AlCl4- + H+ -> AlCl3 + HCl; the product is raspberry ketone.

questions.question: Give a reason why the yield of raspberry ketone by this Friedel-Crafts method is not high.
questions.answer: The OH group of phenol coordinates to and deactivates the AlCl3 catalyst, and side reactions (O-acylation, multiple substitution) lower the yield.
steps: Phenol's OH group (lone pair) bonds to the Lewis acid AlCl3, reducing its activity.
Acylation can occur on O (giving an ester) instead of on the ring.
Polysubstitution and other by-products also reduce the yield of the desired ketone.

questions.question: Devise a multi-step Grignard synthesis of raspberry ketone, giving reagents, conditions and intermediates, including formation of the Grignard reagent.
questions.answer: Step 1: oxidise the primary alcohol to the aldehyde with acidified K2Cr2O7, heating and distilling out the product, giving HOC6H4CH2CH2CHO. Step 2: make CH3MgBr from CH3Br and Mg in dry ether. Step 3: add the aldehyde to CH3MgBr in dry ether, then dilute acid, giving the secondary alcohol HOC6H4CH2CH2CH(OH)CH3. Step 4: oxidise it with acidified K2Cr2O7 (heat under reflux) to raspberry ketone, HOC6H4CH2CH2C(=O)CH3.
steps: The target ketone has one more carbon than the aldehyde, so a Grignard reagent (CH3MgX) must add a CH3 to an aldehyde, and the secondary alcohol formed is then oxidised.
Step 1: acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heat gently and distil off the aldehyde as it forms (to avoid over-oxidation to the acid).
Grignard formation: bromomethane (or iodomethane) with magnesium turnings in dry ether (no water).
Step 2: add the aldehyde to CH3MgBr in dry ether, then dilute acid (or water) to give the secondary alcohol intermediate.
Step 3: acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heated under reflux, oxidises the secondary alcohol to the ketone.
The phenol OH is acidic and also consumes some Grignard reagent, so a slight excess is used.

questions.question: Suggest why the choice of reducing agent is particularly important in the reduction step of the industrial preparation of raspberry ketone.
questions.answer: The reducing agent must reduce only the C=C double bond and leave the C=O group (and the benzene ring) untouched; a stronger or less selective reducing agent such as LiAlH4 or NaBH4 would also reduce the ketone.
steps: The molecule has C=C, C=O and a benzene ring that could all be reduced.
H2 with a suitable catalyst reduces C=C selectively under the mild conditions used.
LiAlH4 or NaBH4 would also reduce the ketone C=O to an alcohol, giving the wrong product.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the stereoisomerism of alpha-ionone and beta-ionone, circling features that give stereoisomerism.
questions.answer: Both molecules show E/Z (geometric) isomerism because the side-chain C=C has two different groups on each carbon (circle the C=C). Only alpha-ionone also shows optical isomerism, because its ring carbon bonded to the side chain is a chiral centre with four different groups (circle that carbon); beta-ionone has no chiral centre.
steps: Similarity: the CH=CH in the side chain of each molecule has two different groups on each carbon, so both can exist as E and Z isomers.

Difference: in alpha-ionone the ring carbon bonded to the side chain has four different groups (H, the side chain, CMe2 and the ring C(CH3)=CH carbon), so it is chiral and gives a pair of enantiomers.
In beta-ionone that carbon is sp2 (part of the ring C=C), so there is no chiral carbon, and the ring C=C cannot show E/Z isomerism because it is in the ring.

questions.question: Identify with an asterisk the carbon environment in alpha-ionone expected to give a quartet in the high resolution proton NMR.
questions.answer: Put the asterisk on the ring CH2 carbon bonded to the =CH carbon (the CH2 at the bottom left of the ring, next to the CH=C(CH3) carbon).
steps: A quartet needs exactly 3 neighbouring hydrogens (n + 1 = 4).
The ring CH2 next to the ring =CH has 1 H on the =CH carbon and 2 H on the other CH2, so 3 neighbours and a quartet.
The other CH2 is next to a carbon with no H, so it would be a triplet; the CH3 groups are all singlets.

questions.question: Predict the number of peaks in the 13C NMR spectrum of the ionone (C13H20O) and justify.
questions.answer: 12 peaks
steps: Beta-ionone has 13 carbons, so there are at most 13 peaks.

The two CH3 groups on the ring carbon C(CH3)2 are in identical environments (they are mirror images across a plane of symmetry through the ring), unlike in alpha-ionone where the chiral centre makes them different.
Every other carbon is different from the rest, so there are 12 different environments and 12 peaks.

questions.question: The formula of a chromium compound is [Cr(H2O)4Cl2]+Cl- (M 230.5). What is the percentage by mass of chlorine in the complex ion? A 18.2, B 30.8, C 36.4, D 46.2%.
steps: Chlorine in the complex ion = 2 x 35.5 = 71.0 (excludes the outer Cl-).

questions.topic: Suitable Liquid for Melting Point Bath
questions.question: Which is a suitable liquid for the beaker used in the melting point apparatus? A deionised water, B ethanol, C hexane, D mineral oil.
questions.answer: D: mineral oil.
steps: The bath must be heated to about 135 C.
Water, ethanol and hexane boil below this temperature.
Mineral oil has a high boiling point, so it is suitable.

questions.question: Which is likely the main impurity in the aspirin sample (melting range 125 C, pure 135 C)? A ethanoic acid, B ethanoic anhydride, C ethanol, D 2-hydroxybenzoic acid.
questions.answer: D: 2-hydroxybenzoic acid (unreacted salicylic acid).
steps: Aspirin is made from salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) and ethanoic anhydride.
Incomplete reaction leaves unreacted salicylic acid as the main impurity.
Impurities lower and broaden the melting point, matching the observed 125 C range.

questions.question: Give the molecular formula of gingerol from its skeletal formula.
steps: Count carbons: benzene ring 6, OCH3 1, chain CH2CH2C(=O)CH2CH(OH)CH2CH2CH2CH2CH3 10 carbons gives 17 C.
Hydrogens: ring 3, phenol OH 1, OCH3 3, CH2CH2 4, CH2 2, CH 1, OH 1, (CH2)4CH3 11 gives 26 H.
Oxygens: phenol OH, OCH3, C=O and alcohol OH gives 4 O, so C17H26O4.

questions.question: The OH group in gingerol is shown attached by a wedge-shaped bond. Suggest why the bond is shown as a wedge.
questions.answer: The wedge shows the bond points towards the viewer, showing the 3D arrangement at the chiral carbon so that the specific enantiomer is identified.
steps: The carbon bearing OH is a chiral centre.
A wedge shows the bond projects out of the plane of the paper.
This specifies one enantiomer (the natural form) rather than a racemic mixture.
So the wedge conveys the 3D configuration of the molecule.

questions.question: Complete the four-step synthesis of zingerone from coniferyl alcohol, with completed intermediate structures and reagents/conditions (Step 2 uses a Grignard reagent; Steps 1, 3 and 4 are redox).
questions.answer: Step 1: acidified K2Cr2O7, heat and distil, gives intermediate 1 Ar-CH=CH-CHO. Step 2: CH3MgBr in dry ether, then dilute acid, gives intermediate 2 Ar-CH=CH-CH(OH)CH3. Step 3: acidified K2Cr2O7, heat under reflux, gives intermediate 3 Ar-CH=CH-C(=O)CH3. Step 4: H2 with Ni (or Rh/Pd) catalyst gives zingerone, Ar-CH2CH2C(=O)CH3 (Ar = 4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl).
steps: Step 1 is oxidation: the primary alcohol CH2OH of coniferyl alcohol becomes the aldehyde CHO (acidified potassium dichromate, heat, distil out the aldehyde); the C=C is kept.
Step 2 is the Grignard step: CH3MgBr (from CH3Br + Mg in dry ether) adds CH3 to the aldehyde, then dilute acid gives the secondary alcohol, Ar-CH=CH-CH(OH)CH3.
Step 3 is oxidation again: acidified potassium dichromate(VI), heat under reflux, turns the secondary alcohol into the ketone Ar-CH=CH-C(=O)CH3.
Step 4 is reduction of the C=C only, using H2 with a metal catalyst (Ni, Pd or Rh), to give zingerone Ar-CH2CH2C(=O)CH3.
The intermediates all keep the 4-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl ring shown on the page.

questions.question: What is the structure of asparagine in aqueous solution at pH 2? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: D: H3N+ group, COOH group and CONH2 unchanged
steps: At pH 2 (strongly acidic) the amine group is protonated: -NH3+.
The carboxylic acid is not ionised at low pH, so it stays as -COOH (the zwitterion with COO- exists near neutral pH).
The amide group is not protonated significantly, so the answer is D.

questions.question: In the high resolution proton NMR of asparagine, what is the splitting pattern for the protons indicated by the arrow? A singlet, B doublet, C triplet, D quartet.
questions.answer: B: doublet
steps: The CH2 protons are on a carbon next to the CH carbon, which has 1 H, so n + 1 = 2.
The other neighbour is the C=O carbon (no H), and the NH2 and COOH protons exchange and do not cause splitting.

questions.question: Which sequence describes recrystallisation? A cold solvent first, B hot solvent then filter soluble impurities and wash, C hot solvent, filter insoluble impurities, then cool and filter, D hot solvent, filter soluble, then cool and filter insoluble.
questions.answer: C
steps: Dissolve the impure solid in the minimum volume of hot solvent.
Filter while hot to remove insoluble impurities.
Cool the solution so the pure compound crystallises, then filter to collect crystals.
Answer C.

questions.question: Complete the table for the outline synthesis of propanoic acid from ethanoic acid, which uses Grignard reagents to lengthen the chain.
questions.answer: Step 1: LiAlH4 in dry ether (then add water/dilute acid). Step 2: HBr (e.g. NaBr + concentrated H2SO4, heat) or PBr3. Compound X: bromoethane, CH3CH2Br. Step 3: Mg in dry ether (heat under reflux). Grignard reagent: CH3CH2MgBr. Step 4: CO2 (solid), then dilute acid.
steps: Step 1 reduces ethanoic acid to ethanol: lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III) in dry ether, followed by dilute acid or water.
Step 2 converts the alcohol to a halogenoalkane, X = bromoethane (HBr from NaBr and concentrated H2SO4, heat; PBr3 is also acceptable).
Step 3 makes the Grignard reagent: bromoethane with magnesium in dry (anhydrous) ether, giving CH3CH2MgBr.
Step 4: CH3CH2MgBr adds to CO2 (solid carbon dioxide, dry ice), then dilute acid gives propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH, with one carbon added.

questions.topic: Molecular Formula of Hydrocarbon from Mass and CO2
questions.question: An 8.4 g hydrocarbon forms 26.4 g CO2 on complete combustion. What is its molecular formula? A CH2, B C6H6, C C2H6, D C6H12.
steps: 26.4 g CO2 = 0.600 mol, so C = 0.600 mol and mass C = 7.2 g.
H mass = 8.4 - 7.2 = 1.2 g; C:H = 0.600 : 1.20 = 1:2, so the empirical formula is CH2.
8.4 g of CH2 units corresponds to 0.100 mol if M = 84 (C6H12), which gives 0.600 mol CO2 = 26.4 g.
Answer D.

questions.question: What are the volumes of oxygen required and carbon dioxide produced at r.t.p. on complete combustion of 5.8 g of butane (Mr 58.0)? Options are in the PDF.
questions.answer: A: 15.6 dm3 of oxygen and 9.6 dm3 of carbon dioxide

questions.question: State the reagents and conditions required for the formation of a diazonium ion from compound A in the synthesis of sunset yellow.
questions.answer: Sodium nitrite with dilute hydrochloric acid at 0-5 C.
steps: Compound A is a primary aromatic amine.
NaNO2 + HCl forms nitrous acid in situ.
Kept at 0-5 C to stop the diazonium ion decomposing.

questions.topic: Structure of Diazonium Ion for Sunset Yellow
questions.question: Draw the structure of the diazonium ion formed from compound A.
questions.answer: The 4-sulfonatobenzenediazonium ion: a benzene ring with N+ triple bond N at one carbon and SO3- Na+ at the carbon opposite (para), with Cl- as the counter-ion.
steps: Diazotisation converts the NH2 group of compound A into N+ triple bond N.
The SO3- Na+ group on the opposite side of the ring is unchanged.

questions.question: Circle the functional group, other than the diazonium group, that is essential for the coupling reaction to occur in sunset yellow.
questions.answer: Circle the OH (hydroxyl, phenol) group on the naphthalene ring, next to the carbon that carries the azo link.
steps: The diazonium ion is a weak electrophile, so it only couples with a ring that is activated.
The OH group donates a lone pair into the ring, activating the ortho position, and the azo group is on the carbon next to the OH.

questions.question: Name the process used to purify sunset yellow after it is formed.
questions.answer: Recrystallisation.
steps: Solid organic products are purified by recrystallisation from a suitable solvent.
This removes impurities such as unreacted starting materials.

questions.topic: Mass of Sunset Yellow from Yield
questions.question: The yield of sunset yellow is 67.9%. Calculate the mass produced from 5.00 g of compound A (Mr of sunset yellow 452.2).
steps: Moles A = 5.00/195.1 = 0.02563 mol, and one mole of A gives one mole of sunset yellow.
Theoretical mass = 0.02563 x 452.2 = 11.59 g.
Actual mass at 67.9% yield = 11.59 x 0.679 = 7.87 g.

questions.question: How many peaks are in the 13C NMR spectrum of 2,2-dimethylpropane? A one, B two, C three, D five.
questions.answer: B: two.
steps: The four CH3 carbons are equivalent: one peak.
The central quaternary C is unique: one peak.
Total 2.

questions.question: Four students sketched the high-resolution proton NMR spectrum of 2,3-dimethylbutane. Which sketch is most likely correct? The sketches are in the PDF.
questions.answer: B
steps: 2,3-Dimethylbutane, (CH3)2CH-CH(CH3)2, has two proton environments: 12 H in four equivalent CH3 groups (doublet) and 2 H in the two equivalent CH groups.
Each CH3 is next to one CH hydrogen, so a doublet near 0.9 ppm; each CH has 6 neighbouring H, giving a septet near 1.4 ppm.
The areas are 12 : 2 (6 : 1), so the doublet is much larger than the multiplet: sketch B.
A is a single peak, C shows a triplet (wrong splitting) and D is too complex.

questions.question: A substituted benzene has general formula CnH2n-6. 0.025 mol produced 11.0 g CO2 on complete combustion. Which could be its Mr? A 64, B 78, C 128, D 134.
steps: Carbon per molecule = 0.250/0.025 = 10, so n = 10.
